orig_binomial_expansion_expansion.description: Build a finite expansion from its coefficient pattern, keep signs and fractions inside their powers, and know exactly what changes after a substitution.

sections.title: Why do the middle coefficients appear?
sections.label: Pattern and Pascal
sections.intro:
A binomial has two terms, such as \(1+x\), \(2-x\) or \(3+\frac{x}{2}\). A positive integer power means multiplying that bracket by itself repeatedly.

\[(1+x)^2=(1+x)(1+x)=1+2x+x^2.\]

The middle coefficient is \(2\) because there are two ways to choose one \(x\) from the two brackets. In \((1+x)^3\), there are three ways to choose exactly one \(x\) and three ways to choose exactly two.

blocks.html: In \((A+B)^n\), choose either \(A\) or \(B\) from each of the \(n\) brackets. Choosing \(B\) from exactly \(r\) brackets produces \(A^{n-r}B^r\). Its binomial coefficient counts how many selections produce that contribution.

For small powers, Pascal’s triangle gives the coefficients. Start with a single \(1\), labelled row \(n=0\). Each later row has \(1\) at both ends; each inside number is the sum of the two numbers above it. Use the row whose label matches the power.

Pascal’s triangle gives the coefficients for \((1+x)^n\). Each interior entry is the sum of the two entries immediately above it.

PowerCoefficients in ascending powers of \(x\)
\(n=0\)\(1\)
\(n=1\)\(1,\ 1\)
\(n=2\)\(1,\ 2,\ 1\)
\(n=3\)\(1,\ 3,\ 3,\ 1\)
\(n=4\)\(1,\ 4,\ 6,\ 4,\ 1\)
\(n=5\)\(1,\ 5,\ 10,\ 10,\ 5,\ 1\)

For example, the two \(3\)s in row \(3\) give \(3+3=6\) in row \(4\).

\[(1+x)^5=1+5x+10x^2+10x^3+5x^4+x^5.\]

Row \(n=4\) gives \(1,4,6,4,1\). The next row gives \(1,5,10,10,5,1\).

blocks.title: Read the row that matches the power
blocks.prompt: In the expansion of \((1+x)^5\), how many nonzero terms are there? Find the coefficient of \(x^2\).

retry.feedback: Include the constant term. The powers are \(0,1,2,3,4,5\).

blocks.hint: The row labelled \(n=5\) starts \(1,5,10\). The constant counts as a term.
blocks.solution:
1. \[(1+x)^5=1+5x+10x^2+10x^3+5x^4+x^5.\]

  2. There are six nonzero terms. The coefficient of \(x^2\) is \(10\); the whole term is \(10x^2\).

blocks.html: The coefficient of \(x^2\) is a number; the term includes the variable. In \(10x^2\), the coefficient is \(10\), not \(10x^2\).

sections.title: How do I expand without repeated multiplication?
sections.label: The binomial rule
sections.intro: Use \(\binom{n}{r}\), also written \({}^{n}C_r\), for a binomial coefficient. The factorial symbol means multiply the positive integers down to one; for example, \(4!=4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1=24\). By definition, \(0!=1\).

blocks.html:
\[\binom{n}{r}=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!},\qquad r=0,1,\ldots,n.\]\[(A+B)^n=\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{n}{r}A^{n-r}B^r.\]

The sum symbol means add the contribution for each listed integer \(r\). Here \(n\) is a positive integer.

Write the coefficients from \(\binom{n}{0}\) to \(\binom{n}{n}\). Alongside them, decrease the power of the complete first term from \(n\) to \(0\), and increase the power of the complete second term from \(0\) to \(n\). Multiply, then simplify each contribution.

\[(A+B)^3=A^3+3A^2B+3AB^2+B^3.\]

The two exponents in each contribution add to \(n\). There are \(n+1\) contributions before simplifying; substitution may make some zero or combine like terms. For \((a+bx)^n\) with nonzero constants \(a,b\), all \(n+1\) powers of \(x\) appear.
For example, \(\binom{6}{2}=\frac{6\cdot5}{2\cdot1}=15\). You can also use the calculator’s combination function. For a full expansion, small Pascal rows are often quicker.

blocks.title: Power the whole second term

retry.feedback: The square applies to both factors: \((3x)^2=9x^2\). Multiply by the binomial coefficient \(3\) afterwards.

blocks.hint: Use the coefficients \(1,3,3,1\), then apply the powers to \(3x\), not only to \(x\).

blocks.html: A calculator can find \({}^{n}C_r\). Show the coefficient multiplied by both complete powers before simplifying; that line makes your method and sign choices clear.

Boundary checks: \(n=1\) gives \(A+B\). For \(n=0\), the expansion is the constant \(1\); as a numerical power, \((A+B)^0=1\) requires \(A+B\ne0\). The assessed finite-expansion method here uses positive integer powers. Fractional or negative outer powers need a different theorem.

sections.title: What changes when a term is negative?
sections.label: Signs and whole terms
sections.intro: Rewrite a subtraction as addition of a negative term. In \((2-x)^4\), use \(2\) and \(-x\). Keep brackets around \(-x\) until its power has been applied.

blocks.html:
\[(-u)^{2k}=u^{2k},\qquad (-u)^{2k+1}=-u^{2k+1}.\]

Even powers remove a negative sign. Odd powers keep it. For positive constants \(a,b\), the coefficients in \((a-bx)^n\) alternate in sign when written in ascending powers of \(x\).

For \((2-x)^4\), keep the minus sign inside the selected factor.

\(r\)\(\binom4r\)\(2^{4-r}\)\((-x)^r\)Term
\(0\)\(1\)\(16\)\(1\)\(16\)
\(1\)\(4\)\(8\)\(-x\)\(-32x\)
\(2\)\(6\)\(4\)\(x^2\)\(24x^2\)
\(3\)\(4\)\(2\)\(-x^3\)\(-8x^3\)
\(4\)\(1\)\(1\)\(x^4\)\(x^4\)
\[(2-x)^4=16-32x+24x^2-8x^3+x^4.\]

For \((2-x)^4\), the coefficient row is \(1,4,6,4,1\). The complete powers produce \(16,-32x,24x^2,-8x^3,x^4\).

blocks.title: Keep the sign inside the power

retry.feedback: An even power removes the negative sign: \((-2x)^2=4x^2\).

blocks.hint: Use \(-2x\) as the complete second term. Its even powers are positive.

blocks.html: Do not put a minus sign in front of every term. Also, \((-x)^2=x^2\) but \(-x^2\) means \(-(x^2)\). The brackets change what is squared.
If the first term is negative too, calculate both signs. For example, \((-1+x)^3=-1+3x-3x^2+x^3\). A memorised “start positive, then alternate” rule does not cover every bracket.

sections.title: What if the first term is not one?
sections.label: Constants and fractions
sections.intro: The same formula works when the first term is \(2\), \(3\) or a fraction. It also works when either term contains a variable. Identify the two complete terms before expanding.

blocks.html:
\[\left(\frac{x}{q}\right)^r=\frac{x^r}{q^r}\qquad(q\ne0).\]

A power applies to every factor in its bracket, including a denominator and a negative sign.

blocks.title: A fractional term must be squared and cubed
blocks.prompt: Write \(\left(2+\frac{x}{2}\right)^3=8+Ax+Bx^2+Cx^3\). Find the three coefficients exactly.
blocks.hint: The middle terms are \(3(2)^2\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\) and \(3(2)\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2\).

blocks.html:
If you factor out a constant before expanding, raise that constant to the outer power too:

\[(a+bx)^n=a^n\left(1+\frac{b}{a}x\right)^n\qquad(a\ne0).\]

The outside factor is \(a^n\), not \(a\). Multiply every term of the resulting expansion by it.

When the variable is in the first term, the direct formula may start with descending powers. For example, expanding \((2x+1)^3\) gives \(8x^3+12x^2+6x+1\). If asked for ascending powers, reorder it as \(1+6x+12x^2+8x^3\).

sections.title: How do I reuse an expansion after substitution?
sections.label: Substitution and order
sections.intro: A formula written using a temporary variable remains true when that variable is replaced by another expression for which the original expressions are defined. Replace it everywhere, use brackets, then simplify the powers.

blocks.html:
1. Let \(y=x^2\), then expand \((1+y)^3=1+3y+3y^2+y^3\).
  2. Replace each power of \(y\) with the corresponding power of \(x\). For example, \(y^3=(x^2)^3=x^6\).
  3. The coefficients follow Pascal row \(n=3\).\[(1+x^2)^3=1+3x^2+3x^4+x^6.\]

Replacing \(y\) by \(x^2\) maps \(1,y,y^2,y^3\) to \(1,x^2,x^4,x^6\). The coefficients stay \(1,3,3,1\).

Ascending powers means the exponent of the stated variable increases from left to right. First three nonzero terms means the first three contributions whose coefficients are not zero; it does not always mean the constant, linear and quadratic terms.

blocks.title: Collect a cancellation before counting terms
blocks.prompt: Find the terms up to and including \(x^3\) in \((1+x-x^2)^3\), in the form \(1+Ax+Bx^2+Cx^3\). Find \(A,B,C\).
blocks.hint: Use \(u=x-x^2\) in \(1+3u+3u^2+u^3\), then combine contributions to each power.
blocks.solution:
1. \[3u=3x-3x^2,\qquad 3u^2=3x^2-6x^3+3x^4.\]
  2. \[u^3=x^3-3x^4+3x^5-x^6.\]

  3. The requested terms combine to \(1+3x+0x^2-5x^3\), so \(A=3\), \(B=0\), \(C=-5\).

  4. Through \(x^2\) there are only two nonzero terms, \(1+3x\). The first three nonzero terms extend to \(-5x^3\).

blocks.title: Substitution changes the powers that appear
blocks.prompt: Expand \((1-3x^2)^3\). Enter the coefficients of \(x^2\), \(x^4\) and \(x^3\), and the highest power of \(x\).

retry.feedback: The outer exponent is \(3\), but the variable is squared inside: \((x^2)^3=x^6\).

blocks.solution:
1. \[(1-3x^2)^3=1+3(-3x^2)+3(-3x^2)^2+(-3x^2)^3.\]
  2. \[=1-9x^2+27x^4-27x^6.\]

  3. No \(x^3\) term appears, so its coefficient is \(0\). The highest power is \(6\).

blocks.html:
For polynomial substitutions, collect all contributions to each requested power before stopping. If the substituted expression has a nonzero constant, later powers can still contribute to low powers of \(x\).

Substitute into the powers as well as the first occurrence: if \(t=-2x^2\), then \(t^2=4x^4\), not \(-2x^4\). A missing power has coefficient \(0\).

Replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) keeps even-power terms unchanged and reverses the signs of odd-power terms. If a substitution contains a fraction or a square root, keep its original domain restriction; expansion does not remove it. Finding a selected term with such substitutions is developed in the next topic.

sections.title: When is the answer exact, and how can I check it?
sections.label: Exactness and checks
sections.intro: For a positive integer power, a complete finite binomial expansion is an identity: it equals the original bracket at every real value allowed by the original expression. For \((a+bx)^n\) with real constants \(a,b\), there is no restriction on \(x\).

blocks.html: “Find the first three terms” asks for part of an expansion. That shorter polynomial is generally not equal to the original expression. To write an exact equality, include the omitted terms or name their exact remainder.

blocks.title: Test an equality after stopping early
blocks.prompt:
Let \(P(x)=(2+x)^4\). Its first three terms in ascending powers of \(x\) form \(Q(x)=16+32x+24x^2\).

Find \(P(1)\) and \(Q(1)\). Is \(P(x)=Q(x)\) true for every real \(x\)?

fields.label: Does the equality hold for every real value?

blocks.hint: Evaluate the original bracket and the shorter polynomial separately at \(x=1\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(1)=3^4=81,\qquad Q(1)=16+32+24=72.\]
  2. \[P(x)=16+32x+24x^2+8x^3+x^4.\]

  3. The omitted terms contribute \(9\) at \(x=1\). One counterexample disproves the claimed equality for every real value.

blocks.html:
Check a full expansion efficiently:

  1. Set \(x=0\): does the constant match the original bracket?
  2. Check the highest power and its coefficient.
  3. Try a convenient value, such as \(x=1\), on both sides to catch sign or arithmetic errors.

A mismatch proves something is wrong. Agreement at one or two values is only a check, not a proof that two polynomials are identical; the expansion method supplies the proof.

Answer the exact request: full expansion, first few terms, a coefficient, or a value. Keep fractions exact unless a numerical accuracy is requested. Write the terms in the requested order before moving on.

glossary.definition: An expression with two terms.
An equivalent expression obtained by multiplying out brackets.
The number multiplying a power of the variable; in \(-12x^2\), it is \(-12\).
The selection count \(\binom{n}{r}\) used before the complete term powers are evaluated.
\(n!=n(n-1)\cdots2\cdot1\) for a positive integer; \(0!=1\).
Terms ordered from the smallest exponent of the stated variable to the largest.
An equality true for every input in its stated domain.
The terms left out when an expansion is stopped early.

examples.title: Build a small expansion from its coefficient row
examples.question: Expand \((1+t)^4\) in ascending powers of \(t\).
solution: Pair it with the powers \(t^0,t^1,t^2,t^3,t^4\). Since \(t^0\) supplies the constant term, write it as \(1\).
The coefficients are the numbers \(1,4,6,4,1\). For example, \(6t^2\) is a term and \(6\) is its coefficient.

examples.title: Use a coefficient, then two complete powers
examples.question: Expand \((1+2x)^4\) completely.
solution: Here the two terms are \(1\) and \(2x\); the power is \(4\).
The binomial coefficient for the square is \(6\), but the coefficient of \(x^2\) in this expansion is \(6\cdot4=24\).

examples.title: Track both the decreasing powers and the negative sign
examples.question: Expand \((2-x)^4\) in ascending powers of \(x\).
solution: The powers of \(2\) decrease from \(4\) to \(0\). The powers of \(-x\) increase from \(0\) to \(4\).
The constant is \(2^4=16\). The last coefficient is positive because \((-x)^4=x^4\).

examples.title: Expand with a fractional second term
examples.question: Expand \(\left(3+\frac{x}{2}\right)^3\), leaving all coefficients exact.
solution: Expanding the unit bracket and multiplying every term by \(27\) gives the same result. Factoring is a choice; the direct formula already handles a first term other than \(1\).

examples.title: The denominator and the sign both have powers
examples.question: Expand \(\left(2-\frac{x}{3}\right)^3\).

examples.title: Replace a temporary variable by a square
examples.question: Use the expansion of \((1+y)^3\) to expand \((1+x^2)^3\).
solution: Ascending powers need not be consecutive. Here the odd powers have coefficient \(0\).

examples.title: Collect powers after a polynomial substitution
examples.question: Find the terms up to and including \(x^3\) in the expansion of \((1+2x-x^2)^4\).
solution:
The lowest power in \(u^4\) is \(x^4\), so it cannot contribute to the requested terms. Collect the powers through \(x^3\):

\[1+8x+(-4+24)x^2+(-24+32)x^3=1+8x+20x^2+8x^3.\]
These are the terms up to and including \(x^3\). Higher powers remain in the full expansion. We could ignore \(u^4\) only because \(u\) has no constant term.

examples.title: Evaluate an expansion with a square root
examples.question: Write \((2+\sqrt{3})^3\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{3}\), where \(a,b\) are integers.
solution: Thus \(a=26\) and \(b=15\). Keep the square root exact and combine like terms.

examples.title: Keep an exact remainder when you stop early
examples.question: For \(P(x)=(1+x)^4\), let \(Q(x)\) be its first three terms in ascending powers of \(x\). Find \(Q(x)\), the exact difference \(P(x)-Q(x)\), and both values at \(x=0.1\).
solution: The full expansion is exact. Using only \(Q\) gives an approximation here; the omitted terms determine its error. A finite binomial identity has no condition such as \(|x|<1\).

extraPractice.title: Use factorial notation for a coefficient
extraPractice.prompt: Find \(\binom{7}{2}\), then state the coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+x)^7\) and the number of nonzero terms in its full expansion.
extraPractice.hint: Cancel the factorials before multiplying. The constant term is included in the count.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\binom{7}{2}=\frac{7!}{2!5!}=\frac{7\cdot6}{2}=21.\]

  2. The \(x^2\) contribution is \(21(1)^5x^2=21x^2\). The powers run from \(0\) through \(7\), giving eight nonzero terms.

extraPractice.title: Expand a scaled linear term
extraPractice.prompt: Write \((1+4x)^3=1+Ax+Bx^2+Cx^3\). Find all three coefficients.

extraPractice.title: Two nonunit terms and a subtraction
extraPractice.prompt: Expand \((3-2x)^3=A+Bx+Cx^2+Dx^3\). Find \(A,B,C,D\).
extraPractice.hint: Use \(3\) and \(-2x\) as the complete terms.

extraPractice.title: The first term can be fractional
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\left(\frac{1}{2}+x\right)^4=A+Bx+Cx^2+Dx^3+x^4\). Find the four coefficients exactly.
extraPractice.hint: Decrease the power of \(\frac{1}{2}\) from \(4\) to \(0\) across the expansion.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\left(\frac{1}{2}+x\right)^4=\frac{1}{16}+4\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)x+6\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)x^2+4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)x^3+x^4.\]
  2. \[=\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{3}{2}x^2+2x^3+x^4.\]

extraPractice.title: A cubed substitution leaves missing powers
extraPractice.prompt: Expand \((2-x^3)^3\). Find the coefficients of \(x^3\), \(x^6\) and \(x^4\), and the highest power of \(x\).
extraPractice.hint: Use \(-x^3\) as the second term, and apply \((x^3)^r=x^{3r}\).

extraPractice.title: Repair an expansion and explain a check
extraPractice.prompt: A student claims \((2-x)^3=8-12x+6x^2-2x^3\). The first three coefficients are correct. Find the correct coefficient of \(x^3\), and the correct value of \((2-x)^3\) at \(x=1\). Would testing only \(x=0\) detect this error?
extraPractice.hint: The final contribution is \((-x)^3\). At \(x=0\), every nonconstant term vanishes.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[(2-x)^3=8-12x+6x^2-x^3.\]
  2. \[(2-1)^3=1,\qquad 8-12+6-1=1.\]

  3. The incorrect polynomial gives \(0\) at \(x=1\), so that value catches the error. Both expressions give \(8\) at \(x=0\); testing only that value would miss it.

starters.title: An exact expansion with a negative fraction
starters.question: Expand \(\left(3-\frac{x}{2}\right)^4\) completely in ascending powers of \(x\). Write your answer as \(81+Ax+Bx^2+Cx^3+Dx^4\), and enter the four coefficients exactly.
starters.hint: Keep \(-\frac{x}{2}\) in brackets until each power is evaluated.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: use the coefficient row \(1,4,6,4,1\) with complete powers.
  • 1 mark: obtain \(-54x\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(\frac{27}{2}x^2\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(-\frac{3}{2}x^3\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(\frac{1}{16}x^4\) and present the complete expansion in ascending powers.

starters.title: Distinguish nonzero terms from consecutive powers
starters.question:
The expansion of \((1+z)^5\) starts \(1+5z+10z^2+10z^3\).

Find the first four nonzero terms of \((1-2x^2)^5\), in ascending powers of \(x\), in the form \(1+Ax^2+Bx^4+Cx^6\). Also give the coefficient of \(x^3\) and the highest power of \(x\) in the full expansion.
starters.hint: Set \(z=-2x^2\). For the highest power, use the final contribution \((-2x^2)^5\).
starters.solution:
1. \[1+5(-2x^2)+10(-2x^2)^2+10(-2x^2)^3=1-10x^2+40x^4-80x^6.\]

  2. Only even powers occur, so the coefficient of \(x^3\) is \(0\).

  3. \[(-2x^2)^5=-32x^{10}.\]

  4. The highest power is \(10\). The two further terms of the full expansion are \(80x^8-32x^{10}\); they are not part of the requested first four terms.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: substitute \(z=-2x^2\) into each complete power.
  • 1 mark: obtain \(-10x^2\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(40x^4\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(-80x^6\).
  • 1 mark: identify the missing \(x^3\) term and give coefficient \(0\).
  • 1 mark: obtain highest power \(10\) from the final contribution.

starters.title: Find exactly what stopping early leaves out
starters.question:
Let \(P(x)=(2-3x)^4\), and let \(Q(x)\) consist of its first three terms in ascending powers of \(x\). Write \(Q(x)=16+Ax+Bx^2\) and \(P(x)-Q(x)=Cx^3+Dx^4\).

Find \(A,B,C,D\), then calculate the exact difference \(P\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)-Q\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)\).
starters.hint: Find all five contributions before separating the first three from the remainder.
starters.solution:
1. \[P(x)=16+4(8)(-3x)+6(4)(-3x)^2+4(2)(-3x)^3+(-3x)^4.\]
  2. \[P(x)=16-96x+216x^2-216x^3+81x^4.\]
  3. \[Q(x)=16-96x+216x^2,\qquad P(x)-Q(x)=-216x^3+81x^4.\]
  4. \[P\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)-Q\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)=-\frac{216}{1000}+\frac{81}{10000}=-\frac{2079}{10000}.\]

  5. The negative difference means the first-three-term value is larger than the exact value at this input.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: use complete binomial contributions with \(2\) and \(-3x\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(A=-96\) and \(B=216\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(C=-216\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(D=81\).
  • 1 mark: substitute \(x=\frac{1}{10}\) into the exact remainder.
  • 1 mark: simplify to \(-\frac{2079}{10000}\).

starters.title: Use the expansion for an exact surd value
starters.question: Use a binomial expansion to express \((3-\sqrt{2})^3\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{2}\), where \(a,b\) are integers.
starters.hint: Use complete terms \(3\) and \(-\sqrt{2}\). The square is positive; the cube is negative.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: use the four binomial contributions with complete terms.
  • 1 mark: evaluate \((-\sqrt{2})^2=2\) and \((-\sqrt{2})^3=-2\sqrt{2}\).
  • 1 mark: combine the rational terms to obtain \(45\).
  • 1 mark: combine the square-root terms to obtain \(-29\sqrt{2}\).

revision.body:
Choose the two complete terms; keep their powers and signs together.

The finite rule

\[(A+B)^n=\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{n}{r}A^{n-r}B^r.\]\[\binom{n}{r}=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!},\qquad 0!=1.\]

Positive integer \(n\); \(r=0,1,\ldots,n\). Powers add to \(n\). There are \(n+1\) contributions before simplification.

Small rows and complete powers

Pascal rows: \(n=3:\ 1,3,3,1\); \(n=4:\ 1,4,6,4,1\).

\[(A+B)^3=A^3+3A^2B+3AB^2+B^3.\]

Power the whole term: \((-2x)^2=4x^2\), \(\left(-\frac{x}{3}\right)^3=-\frac{x^3}{27}\). Factoring \(a\) from a bracket raised to \(n\) puts \(a^n\) outside.

Signs, substitution and order

\[(2-x)^4=16-32x+24x^2-8x^3+x^4.\]\[(1+x^2)^3=1+3x^2+3x^4+x^6.\]

After polynomial substitution, collect each power before truncating. Ascending powers can have gaps; missing coefficients are \(0\). Keep surds exact and preserve original domain restrictions.

Exactness and checks

A full positive-integer expansion is exact throughout its original domain. First few terms omit a remainder; do not present them as the full identity. Check the constant at \(x=0\), the highest power, and a convenient input. Matching one value does not prove an identity.

\(n=1\): the bracket itself. \(n=0\): the constant \(1\), with nonzero base for numerical exponentiation.
revision.checks:
• Right Pascal row or combination?
  • Both complete terms raised to their powers?
  • Signs, denominators and substitutions correct?
  • Requested order, number of terms and exactness clear?

orig_binomial_expansion_general_term.description: Find only the term you need. Match its exponent, check its index, then calculate its coefficient with every sign and domain restriction intact.

sections.title: Which index gives the requested term?
sections.label: Index and term number
sections.intro: When you need one term, a full expansion is unnecessary. The general term describes one contribution for each integer index \(r\).

blocks.html:
\[T_{r+1}=\binom{n}{r}A^{n-r}B^r,\qquad r=0,1,\ldots,n.\]

Use the two complete terms \(A,B\) exactly as written. The first contribution uses \(r=0\), so its term number is \(r+1\).

In \((2+x)^5\), the term at index \(r\) is \(T_{r+1}=\binom5r2^{5-r}x^r\).

\(r\)Term number\(\binom5r\)\(2^{5-r}\)Term
\(0\)\(1\)\(1\)\(32\)\(32\)
\(1\)\(2\)\(5\)\(16\)\(80x\)
\(2\)\(3\)\(10\)\(8\)\(80x^2\)

The third term uses \(r=2\). Its binomial coefficient is \(\binom52=10\), and the coefficient of \(x^2\) is \(10\times8=80\).

For \((2+x)^5\), indices \(0,1,2\) correspond to terms \(T_1,T_2,T_3\). The binomial coefficients \(1,5,10\) become final coefficients \(32,80,80\) after the powers of \(2\) are included.

blocks.title: Turn a position into an index
blocks.prompt: Find the fourth term in the standard binomial order of \((1-2x)^5\). Give its index \(r\), coefficient and power of \(x\).

retry.feedback: The term number is \(r+1\), so the fourth term uses \(r=3\).

blocks.hint: The first term has index \(0\). The fourth term therefore uses \(r=3\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[T_4=\binom{5}{3}(1)^2(-2x)^3=10(-8x^3)=-80x^3.\]

  2. The index is \(3\), the coefficient is \(-80\), and the power is \(3\).

blocks.html: The fifth term uses \(r=4\), not \(5\). Also, “term number” needs an ordering: the standard formula starts with \(A^n\); ascending powers of \(x\) may use a different order.

sections.title: How do I select a coefficient?
sections.label: Match the power
sections.intro: Write the general contribution, simplify its power of the requested variable, then set that exponent equal to the target. Check that the resulting index is an integer between \(0\) and \(n\). Only then calculate its coefficient.

blocks.html:
\[(ax^p+bx^q)^n:\quad T_{r+1}=\binom{n}{r}a^{n-r}b^r x^{p(n-r)+qr}.\]\[\text{Exponent}=pn+(q-p)r.\]

For target \(x^m\), solve \(pn+(q-p)r=m\). When \(p\ne q\), at most one index can give that exponent.

blocks.title: Find one coefficient without a full expansion
blocks.prompt: Find the coefficient of \(x^4\) in \((2+3x)^6\). Give the required index and the coefficient.

retry.feedback: \(15\) is only the binomial coefficient. Also multiply by \(2^2\) and \(3^4\).

blocks.hint: The power of \(x\) is \(r\). Evaluate \(\binom{6}{4}2^2 3^4\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[T_{r+1}=\binom{6}{r}2^{6-r}(3x)^r.\]
  2. \[r=4,\qquad T_5=\binom{6}{4}2^2 3^4x^4=4860x^4.\]

  3. The requested coefficient is \(4860\), without the \(x^4\).

blocks.html: A coefficient is the number multiplying the requested power. A term includes that power. For example, the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \(-720x^3\) is \(-720\).
Show the exponent equation and the selected coefficient product. A calculator can evaluate \(\binom{n}{r}\), but it cannot decide which index matches the question for you.

sections.title: How do negative powers and constant terms work?
sections.label: Laurent powers and missing terms
sections.intro: A finite expression containing negative integer powers, such as \(x^2+x^{-1}\), is sometimes called a Laurent polynomial. Rewrite reciprocals as powers before combining exponents. Negative powers require \(x\ne0\).

blocks.html:
In \(\left(2x^2-\frac1x\right)^5\) with \(x\ne0\), the power of \(x\) is \(2(5-r)-r=10-3r\).

\(r\)Power
\(0\)\(x^{10}\)
\(1\)\(x^{7}\)
\(2\)\(x^{4}\)
\(3\)\(x^{1}\)
\(4\)\(x^{-2}\)
\(5\)\(x^{-5}\)
  1. For \(x^4\), solve \(10-3r=4\implies r=2\).\[T_3=\binom52 2^3(-1)^2x^4=80x^4.\]
  2. A constant term would require \(10-3r=0\implies r=\frac{10}{3}\). The index must be an integer from \(0\) to \(5\), so there is no constant term.

The exponent \(10-3r\) takes only \(10,7,4,1,-2,-5\) for \(r=0,1,\ldots,5\). The power \(4\) is present; the power \(0\) is not.

“Independent of \(x\)” means exponent \(0\). Solve the exponent equation; do not substitute \(x=0\) into an expression with a denominator.

If the required index is fractional, negative or greater than \(n\), that power is absent and its coefficient is \(0\).

blocks.title: A constant may appear while another power is missing
blocks.prompt: In \(\left(x^3-\frac{2}{x}\right)^4\), where \(x\ne0\), find the index of the constant term, its coefficient, and the coefficient of \(x^2\).

retry.feedback: A constant needs exponent zero, not index zero. Solve \(12-4r=0\).

blocks.hint: The exponent is \(3(4-r)-r=12-4r\). Match it to \(0\), then to \(2\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[T_{r+1}=\binom{4}{r}(-2)^r x^{12-4r}.\]
  2. \[12-4r=0\Longrightarrow r=3,\qquad T_4=4(-2)^3=-32.\]
  3. \[12-4r=2\Longrightarrow r=\frac{5}{2}.\]

  4. The second index is not an integer, so no \(x^2\) term occurs. Its coefficient is \(0\).

blocks.html: For \(x^k(ax^p+bx^q)^n\), include the outside shift \(k\): match \(k+pn+(q-p)r\) to the target. It changes the power, not the coefficient.

sections.title: What if the bracket contains a square root?
sections.label: Fractional powers and domains
sections.intro: The outer power is still a positive integer, so the expansion is finite. Write roots as rational powers and use the same index method. The original expression decides which real inputs are allowed.

blocks.html: For real square roots, \(\sqrt{x}\) requires \(x\ge0\). If \(x\) or \(\sqrt{x}\) also occurs in a denominator, exclude zero. Thus both \(\sqrt{x}+\frac{2}{x}\) and \(\sqrt{x}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\) require \(x>0\).

blocks.title: Keep the original square-root domain
blocks.prompt: Find the constant term in \(\left(\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{x}\right)^6\). State its index and the real domain of the original expression.
blocks.hint: The square root requires \(x\ge0\), and the denominator excludes zero. The combined exponent is \(3-\frac{3r}{2}\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[T_{r+1}=\binom{6}{r}(-1)^r x^{\frac{6-r}{2}-r}=\binom{6}{r}(-1)^r x^{3-\frac{3r}{2}}.\]
  2. \[3-\frac{3r}{2}=0\Longrightarrow r=2,\qquad T_3=\binom{6}{2}=15.\]

  3. The original real domain is \(x>0\); finding a constant contribution does not remove that restriction.

blocks.html: Do not confuse a fractional power of \(x\) inside the bracket with a fractional outer power. Here \(\left(\sqrt{x}+\frac{2}{x}\right)^6\) has six factors and a finite expansion. This lesson does not use the infinite binomial theorem for fractional outer powers.

sections.title: How do I check the order and keep every valid case?
sections.label: Order and complete cases
sections.intro: The exponent changes by \(q-p\) when \(r\) increases by one. If \(q-p>0\), the formula order is ascending. If \(q-p<0\), reverse it for ascending powers. Check the variable named in the question.

blocks.title: Ascending order can reverse the index order
blocks.prompt: Write the first two terms of \(\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)^3\) in ascending powers of \(x\), where \(x\ne0\). Give each coefficient and exponent.
blocks.hint: The exponents in binomial index order are \(3,1,-1,-3\). Start at the smallest exponent for ascending order.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)^3=x^3+3x+\frac{3}{x}+\frac{1}{x^3}.\]

  2. In ascending powers, the first two terms are \(x^{-3}+3x^{-1}\). Their coefficients are \(1,3\), and their exponents are \(-3,-1\).

blocks.html:
If \(p=q\), every contribution has the same power and must be combined:

\[(ax^p+bx^p)^n=(a+b)^n x^{pn}.\]

For example, \((2x-x)^4=x^4\). One selected contribution does not give the final coefficient because all five contributions belong to the same power.

An allowed exponent index can still produce coefficient zero when a parameter is zero. When comparing coefficients, write their expressions first and solve the resulting equation without dividing away a possible zero.

Check the index, original domain, term order and any parameter conditions. Substitute candidate parameter values back into the original coefficient relation. A statement that one coefficient is a multiple of another may allow both to be zero; a ratio requires a nonzero denominator.

glossary.definition: The integer \(r\) choosing one contribution, from \(0\) to \(n\).
The position \(r+1\) in the chosen standard binomial order.
A formula describing each contribution as its index varies.
A contribution with exponent \(0\), independent of the variable.
A finite sum that may contain negative integer powers.
A power with final coefficient zero because no valid contribution produces it.
The set of real inputs for which the original expression is defined.

examples.title: The fifth term has index four
examples.question: Find the fifth term in the standard binomial order of \((2+x)^6\).
solution: The first term uses \(r=0\), so the fifth uses \(r=4\).
Report the whole term \(60x^4\). Its coefficient alone is \(60\).

examples.title: Match the power before calculating the number
examples.question: Find the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \((3-2x)^5\).
solution: The power of \(x\) is \(r\). To obtain \(x^3\), set \(r=3\).
The coefficient is \(-720\). The minus sign comes from an odd power of \(-2\).

examples.title: Both terms contribute to the exponent
examples.question: Find the coefficient of \(x^4\) in \(\left(2x^2-\frac{1}{x}\right)^5\), where \(x\ne0\). Does the expansion have a constant term?
solution: The coefficient is \(80\). A constant would require \(10-3r=0\), so \(r=\frac{10}{3}\). This is not an integer; the constant coefficient is \(0\).

examples.title: A constant term is found by setting the exponent to zero
examples.question: Find the term independent of \(x\) in \(\left(3x-\frac{2}{x^2}\right)^6\), where \(x\ne0\).
solution: This is an integer from \(0\) through \(6\), so it selects an actual contribution.
The constant term is \(4860\). We did not put \(x=0\), which is outside the original domain.

examples.title: An outside power shifts every exponent
examples.question: Find the constant term in \(x^2\left(2x-\frac{1}{x}\right)^4\), where \(x\ne0\).
solution: A contribution from the bracket has exponent \(4-2r\). Multiplication by \(x^2\) changes it to \(6-2r\).

examples.title: A fractional exponent still gives a linear index equation
examples.question: Find the constant term in \(\left(\sqrt{x}+\frac{2}{x}\right)^6\), for \(x>0\).
solution: The allowed index is an integer even though the exponent formula contains a fraction. The original domain remains \(x>0\).

examples.title: Choose the order after identifying the powers
examples.question: Find the first three terms in ascending powers of \(x\) of \(\left(x^2+\frac{1}{x}\right)^4\), where \(x\ne0\).
solution: For \(r=0,1,2,3,4\), the exponents are \(8,5,2,-1,-4\). Ascending powers therefore start at \(r=4\), then \(3\), then \(2\).

examples.title: Keep a zero parameter as a possible solution
examples.question: In \(\left(2x+\frac{a}{x^2}\right)^6\), where \(x\ne0\), the constant coefficient is \(\frac{5}{4}\) times the coefficient of \(x^3\). Find all real values of \(a\).
solution: The constant uses \(r=2\); its coefficient is \(15\cdot16a^2=240a^2\). The \(x^3\) term uses \(r=1\); its coefficient is \(6\cdot32a=192a\).

At \(a=0\), both compared coefficients are zero, so the stated equality still holds. Dividing by \(a\) would lose this valid solution. At \(a=1\), the coefficients are \(240\) and \(192\), which also satisfy the condition.

extraPractice.title: A specified term with a negative second term
extraPractice.prompt: Find the third term in the standard binomial order of \((3-x)^7\). Give its index and coefficient.
extraPractice.hint: Use \(r=2\), so the negative sign is squared.

extraPractice.title: A power substitution creates gaps
extraPractice.prompt: Find the coefficients of \(x^6\) and \(x^7\) in \((1-2x^2)^5\).
extraPractice.hint: The exponent is \(2r\). Solve one index equation for each target.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[T_{r+1}=\binom{5}{r}(-2)^r x^{2r}.\]
  2. \[2r=6\Longrightarrow r=3,\qquad \binom{5}{3}(-2)^3=-80.\]
  3. \[2r=7\Longrightarrow r=\frac{7}{2}.\]

  4. The second index is not an integer, so the \(x^7\) coefficient is \(0\).

extraPractice.title: An integer index can still be out of range
extraPractice.prompt: In \(\left(2x^3+\frac{1}{x^2}\right)^4\), where \(x\ne0\), find the coefficient of \(x^2\) and the coefficient of \(x^{-13}\). Why is the second coefficient zero?

fields.label: Reason for the missing second power

options.bounds: Its required index is greater than the outer power.
options.fractional: Its required index is not an integer.

extraPractice.hint: The exponent is \(12-5r\), with \(r=0,1,2,3,4\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[12-5r=2\Longrightarrow r=2,\qquad \binom{4}{2}2^2=24.\]
  2. \[12-5r=-13\Longrightarrow r=5.\]

  3. The allowed indices stop at \(4\). Thus \(x^{-13}\) is absent and its coefficient is \(0\).

extraPractice.title: Include an outside exponent in a constant-term question
extraPractice.prompt: Find the constant term in \(x^3\left(x-\frac{2}{x}\right)^5\), where \(x\ne0\). Give the selected index and the constant coefficient.
extraPractice.hint: The exponent after the outside multiplication is \(3+(5-r)-r\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[x^3T_{r+1}=\binom{5}{r}(-2)^r x^{8-2r}.\]
  2. \[8-2r=0\Longrightarrow r=4.\]
  3. \[\text{Constant term}=\binom{5}{4}(-2)^4=80.\]

extraPractice.title: Select two powers in a square-root expression
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x>0\), find the constant term and the coefficient of \(x^{-2}\) in \(\left(\sqrt{x}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\right)^8\).
extraPractice.hint: The exponent simplifies to \(4-r\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[T_{r+1}=\binom{8}{r}x^{\frac{8-r}{2}-\frac{r}{2}}=\binom{8}{r}x^{4-r}.\]
  2. \[4-r=0\Longrightarrow r=4,\qquad \binom{8}{4}=70.\]
  3. \[4-r=-2\Longrightarrow r=6,\qquad \binom{8}{6}=28.\]

extraPractice.title: Combine contributions with the same power
extraPractice.prompt: Find the coefficients of \(x^{10}\) and \(x^8\) in \((2x^2-x^2)^5\).
extraPractice.hint: Simplify the two like terms inside the bracket before raising the result to the fifth power.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[(2x^2-x^2)^5=(x^2)^5=x^{10}.\]

  2. The coefficient of \(x^{10}\) is \(1\), and the coefficient of \(x^8\) is \(0\). All binomial contributions have power \(10\), so a single contribution would not give the final coefficient.

starters.title: Select three powers in a Laurent expansion
starters.question: For \(x\ne0\), find the coefficients of \(x^3\), \(x^0\) and \(x^4\) in \(\left(3x^2-\frac{2}{x}\right)^6\). Show the index equation used for each target.
starters.hint: Combine both powers of \(x\) before setting the exponent equal to each target.
starters.solution:
1. \[T_{r+1}=\binom{6}{r}3^{6-r}(-2)^r x^{12-3r}.\]
  2. \[12-3r=3\Longrightarrow r=3,\qquad \binom{6}{3}3^3(-2)^3=-4320.\]
  3. \[12-3r=0\Longrightarrow r=4,\qquad \binom{6}{4}3^2(-2)^4=2160.\]
  4. \[12-3r=4\Longrightarrow r=\frac{8}{3}.\]

  5. The last index is not an integer, so the \(x^4\) coefficient is \(0\).
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain the general coefficient and exponent \(12-3r\).
  • 1 mark: select \(r=3\) for \(x^3\).
  • 1 mark: obtain coefficient \(-4320\).
  • 1 mark: select \(r=4\) and obtain constant \(2160\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(r=\frac{8}{3}\) for the last target.
  • 1 mark: reject the noninteger index and state coefficient \(0\).

starters.title: Use fractional powers and report the correct position
starters.question: For \(x>0\), find the constant coefficient and the coefficient of \(x^{-3}\) in \(\left(2\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{x}\right)^6\). State the term number of the \(x^{-3}\) contribution in standard binomial order.
starters.hint: The exponent is \(3-\frac{3r}{2}\). The coefficient also contains \(2^{6-r}\).
starters.solution:
1. \[T_{r+1}=\binom{6}{r}2^{6-r}(-1)^r x^{3-\frac{3r}{2}}.\]
  2. \[3-\frac{3r}{2}=0\Longrightarrow r=2,\qquad \binom{6}{2}2^4=240.\]
  3. \[3-\frac{3r}{2}=-3\Longrightarrow r=4,\qquad \binom{6}{4}2^2=60.\]

  4. The latter contribution has term number \(r+1=5\), so it is \(T_5=60x^{-3}\).
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain the general coefficient and exponent.
  • 1 mark: select \(r=2\) for the constant.
  • 1 mark: obtain constant \(240\).
  • 1 mark: select \(r=4\) and obtain coefficient \(60\).
  • 1 mark: report term number \(5\).

starters.title: Find all parameter values, including a zero case
starters.question: In \(\left(x^2+\frac{k}{x}\right)^6\), where \(x\ne0\), the constant coefficient equals four times the coefficient of \(x^6\). Find all real values of \(k\).
starters.hint: The constant uses \(r=4\); the \(x^6\) contribution uses \(r=2\). Factor the resulting equation without dividing by \(k\).
starters.solution:
1. \[T_{r+1}=\binom{6}{r}k^r x^{12-3r}.\]
  2. \[\text{Constant coefficient}=15k^4,\qquad \text{coefficient of }x^6=15k^2.\]
  3. \[15k^4=4(15k^2)\Longrightarrow k^2(k^2-4)=0.\]
  4. \[k=0,\quad k=-2,\quad k=2.\]

  5. At \(k=0\), both coefficients are zero. At either nonzero value, the coefficients are \(240\) and \(60\). Every listed value satisfies the stated equality.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: select indices \(4\) and \(2\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(15k^4\) and \(15k^2\).
  • 1 mark: form and factor the coefficient equation.
  • 1 mark: find the nonzero values \(-2,2\).
  • 1 mark: retain and verify the valid zero value.

revision.body:
Match the exponent first. Calculate the coefficient only after checking the index.

General term and position

\[T_{r+1}=\binom{n}{r}A^{n-r}B^r,\qquad r=0,1,\ldots,n.\]

The first contribution has \(r=0\); the \(j\)th has \(r=j-1\). Keep both complete terms inside their powers.

Select a power

\[(ax^p+bx^q)^n:\quad T_{r+1}=\binom{n}{r}a^{n-r}b^r x^{pn+(q-p)r}.\]

For \(x^m\), solve \(pn+(q-p)r=m\). Include an outside factor \(x^k\) by adding \(k\) to the exponent. A constant has \(m=0\).

Reject noninteger or out-of-range indices: that power is absent. An allowed index can still have a zero coefficient.

Domain and order

Negative integer powers: \(x\ne0\). Square root: \(x\ge0\); a denominator may exclude zero. Preserve the original domain.

Exponent step \(q-p>0\): formula order is ascending. Step \(q-p<0\): reverse it. If \(p=q\), combine the like terms inside the bracket first.

One useful model and final checks

\[\left(2x^2-\frac{1}{x}\right)^5:\quad T_{r+1}=\binom{5}{r}2^{5-r}(-1)^r x^{10-3r}.\]

For \(x^4\): \(r=2\), coefficient \(80\). For a constant: \(r=\frac{10}{3}\), so none occurs.

Report a coefficient without its variable. Solve parameter equations without dividing away zero; recheck every candidate in the original relation.
revision.checks:
• Integer index inside the bounds?
  • Both powers and any outside shift included?
  • Correct sign and complete numerical coefficient?
  • Domain, ordering and zero cases checked?

orig_binomial_expansion_products.description: Find a coefficient by matching the powers that can produce it. Keep every contribution, use zero coefficients for gaps, and simplify opposite-sign factors when their structure allows it.

sections.title: Which products can make the required power?
sections.label: Match exponent pairs
sections.intro: Multiplying expansions means choosing one term from each factor. Their coefficients multiply, and their exponents add. Several different pairs can produce the same final power, so add every contributing product.

blocks.html:
\[(a_ix^i)(b_jx^j)=a_i b_j x^{i+j}.\]

For the coefficient of \(x^m\), list all available exponent pairs with \(i+j=m\). Multiply each pair of coefficients, then add the results.

blocks.title: Collect every pair that makes the target power
blocks.prompt: Find the coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1-3x+2x^2)(4+2x-x^2)\). How many nonzero term pairs contribute to it?

retry.feedback: The linear-by-linear product is only one contribution. Include constant-by-quadratic products from both directions.

blocks.hint: Use exponent pairs \((0,2),(1,1),(2,0)\), one exponent from each factor.
blocks.solution:
1. \[1(-x^2)+(-3x)(2x)+(2x^2)(4)=(-1-6+8)x^2=x^2.\]

  2. There are three nonzero pairs. Their coefficients add to \(1\).

blocks.html:
The notation \([x^m]P(x)\) means “the coefficient of \(x^m\) in \(P(x)\)”. It is a label for a coefficient, not multiplication or evaluation. For ordinary polynomials:

\[[x^m](AB)=a_0b_m+a_1b_{m-1}+\cdots+a_mb_0.\]

Here \(a_i,b_j\) are the coefficients in the two factors. Treat a missing power as coefficient \(0\). You can use a small pair list instead of memorising this formula.
The coefficient of \(x^m\) in a product is generally not the product of the two \(x^m\) coefficients: that pair produces \(x^{2m}\). Include constant-by-target contributions as well.

sections.title: How does a linear multiplier change the target?
sections.label: A linear multiplier
sections.intro: Let \(C_j\) be the coefficient of \(x^j\) in \(F(x)\). In \((a+bx)F(x)\), the constant \(a\) leaves exponents unchanged, while \(bx\) raises each exponent by one.

blocks.html:
\[[x^m]\bigl((a+bx)F(x)\bigr)=aC_m+bC_{m-1}.\]

Use the coefficient one power lower for the linear multiplier. For an ordinary polynomial, an index below zero has coefficient \(0\).

To find the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \((1+2x)(1+x)^4\), select every pair of powers adding to \(3\).

First factorSecond factorProduct
\(1\)\(4x^3\)\(4x^3\)
\(2x\)\(6x^2\)\(12x^3\)

The first factor has only two terms, so the complete coefficient is \(4+12=16\).

To reach \(x^3\) in \((1+2x)(1+x)^4\), use \(1\cdot4x^3\) and \(2x\cdot6x^2\). Their coefficients sum to \(16\).

blocks.title: A linear multiplier shifts the required coefficient
blocks.prompt: Find the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \((3-x)(1+2x)^4\). Give the contribution from \(3\), the contribution from \(-x\), and their total.

retry.feedback: Multiplication by \(x\) raises the power by one. Use the \(x^2\) term, not the \(x^3\) term.

blocks.hint: You need the \(x^3\) coefficient and the \(x^2\) coefficient of \((1+2x)^4\).

blocks.html: Write the two contributing products before adding their coefficients. This shows which shifted powers you selected and makes a missed sign easy to find.

sections.title: How do I handle a polynomial multiplier or a missing power?
sections.label: More multiplier terms
sections.intro: Each extra term in a multiplier adds another possible shift. For a quadratic multiplier, use three coefficients from the expanded factor.

blocks.html:
\[[x^m]\bigl((a+bx+cx^2)F(x)\bigr)=aC_m+bC_{m-1}+cC_{m-2}.\]

A gap in the multiplier gives a zero contribution, not a change in the other indices.

blocks.title: A quadratic multiplier gives three contributions
blocks.prompt: Find the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \((1-2x+x^2)(1+3x)^3\).
blocks.hint: The needed coefficients from the binomial are those of \(x^3,x^2,x\).

blocks.html:
For example, \((1+x^2)F(x)\) uses \(C_m+C_{m-2}\); there is no \(C_{m-1}\) contribution because the multiplier has no linear term. Likewise, if \(F(x)=(1+x^2)^n\), its odd-power coefficients are zero.

An outside factor \(x^k\) shifts the whole target: the coefficient of \(x^m\) in \(x^kP(x)\) is the coefficient of \(x^{m-k}\) in \(P(x)\). Account for that shift before listing pairs. A negative outside power raises the required inner power: for \(x\ne0\), \([x^2]\left(\frac{P(x)}{x}\right)=[x^3]P(x)\).
A final coefficient can be zero because no valid pair exists, or because nonzero contributions cancel. Do the pair calculation before deciding which explanation applies.

sections.title: How much of each binomial expansion do I need?
sections.label: Two binomial factors
sections.intro: For \((a+bx)^n(c+dx)^p\), select the necessary coefficients from each factor using the binomial theorem. Pair exponents that sum to the target and include each pair exactly once.

blocks.title: Pair terms from two binomial expansions
blocks.prompt: Find the coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+x)^4(1-2x)^3\).
blocks.hint: Use \((0,2),(1,1),(2,0)\). Terms above degree two cannot contribute because both factors contain only nonnegative powers.
blocks.solution:
1. The required coefficients from the first factor are \(1,4,6\); those from the second are \(1,-6,12\).

  2. \[1(12)+4(-6)+6(1)=12-24+6=-6.\]

blocks.html:
If both factors contain only nonnegative powers, terms above degree \(m\) cannot contribute to \(x^m\). You may stop each expansion there for that coefficient calculation.

If negative powers occur, list the pairs first. A higher power in one factor can combine with a negative power in the other to reach a lower target.

A truncated coefficient list can give an exact selected coefficient even though it is not the full expansion. Label it as the terms needed for the calculation, and keep the original domain if reciprocals occur.

sections.title: Can symmetry or factorisation remove most of the work?
sections.label: Odd and even powers
sections.intro: Replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) changes the sign of every odd power and leaves every even power unchanged. This gives a quick way to see cancellations. These are consequences of algebra; you can derive them instead of learning extra coefficient identities.

blocks.html: For a polynomial \(F\), adding \(F(x)+F(-x)\) cancels odd powers and doubles even-power coefficients. Subtracting \(F(x)-F(-x)\) cancels even powers and doubles odd-power coefficients.

blocks.title: Adding and subtracting keep different powers
blocks.prompt:
Let \(F(x)=(1+2x)^4+(1-2x)^4\) and \(G(x)=(1+2x)^4-(1-2x)^4\).

Find the coefficients of \(x^3\) and \(x^2\) in \(F\), and the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \(G\).
blocks.hint: Replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) reverses odd-power signs and keeps even-power signs.
blocks.solution:
1. In \((1+2x)^4\), the coefficients of \(x^2\) and \(x^3\) are \(24\) and \(32\). In \((1-2x)^4\), they are \(24\) and \(-32\).

  2. \[F:\quad x^3\text{ coefficient}=32-32=0,\quad x^2\text{ coefficient}=24+24=48.\]
  3. \[G:\quad x^3\text{ coefficient}=32-(-32)=64.\]

blocks.html: A product needs a different argument. When opposite-sign brackets have the same positive integer outer power, combine them first:

\[(a+b)^n(a-b)^n=(a^2-b^2)^n.\]

In particular, \((1+cx)^n(1-cx)^n=(1-c^2x^2)^n\), so only even powers of \(x\) occur.

1. Use the matched powers to combine the two brackets.\[(1+x)^4(1-x)^4=(1-x^2)^4.\]
  2. \[(1-x^2)^4=1-4x^2+6x^4-4x^6+x^8.\]The coefficient of \(x^4\) is \(6\) and the coefficient of \(x^3\) is zero.
  3. Direct multiplication confirms that the contributions to \(x^3\) cancel.\[1(-4)+4(6)+6(-4)+4(1)=0.\]

Equal fourth powers combine to \((1-x^2)^4\). Its powers are \(0,2,4,6,8\), so every odd-power coefficient is \(0\).

blocks.title: Combine equal opposite-sign powers first
blocks.prompt: Find the coefficients of \(x^4\) and \(x^3\) in \((1+3x)^3(1-3x)^3\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[(1+3x)^3(1-3x)^3=(1-9x^2)^3.\]

  2. The \(x^4\) contribution is \(\binom{3}{2}(-9x^2)^2=243x^4\). Only even powers occur, so the \(x^3\) coefficient is \(0\).

blocks.html: Do not apply the equal-power shortcut unchanged to unequal powers. Pair the common number of factors, then keep and multiply the leftover factor. Also distinguish a sum from a product: they produce cancellations for different reasons.

glossary.definition: One pair of multiplied terms that produces the target power.
The exponent requested in the question.
A factor whose terms shift powers in another expansion.
A power whose coefficient is zero in the stated expression.
Whether an integer exponent is odd or even.
Contributions of opposite signs adding to zero.
Keeping only a specified part of an expansion.

examples.title: A coefficient comes from a sum of products
examples.question: Find the coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+2x+3x^2)(2-x+4x^2)\).
solution: A product has power \(2\) only when its exponents add to \(2\). The pairs are \((0,2),(1,1),(2,0)\).
No other pair of terms can produce \(x^2\), so the remaining products need not be calculated.

examples.title: A linear factor needs two neighbouring coefficients
examples.question: Find the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \((1+2x)(1+x)^4\).
solution: The constant \(1\) needs an \(x^3\) term from the binomial; the \(2x\) needs an \(x^2\) term.

examples.title: A quadratic factor needs three neighbouring coefficients
examples.question: Find the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \((2+x-x^2)(1-x)^5\).
solution: Match them to the multiplier terms \(2,x,-x^2\), respectively.
The last contribution is positive because both participating coefficients are negative.

examples.title: Two expanded brackets have several valid pairs
examples.question: Find the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \((1+3x)^3(1-x)^4\).
solution: The first factor has coefficients \(1,9,27,27\). The second has coefficients \(1,-4,6,-4,1\), listed from the constant upwards.
The coefficient is \(-31\). Include the constant contribution from each end of the list.

examples.title: A negative power can bring a higher power down
examples.question: Find the coefficient of \(x\) in \((1+x)^5\left(1-\frac{1}{x^2}\right)\), where \(x\ne0\).
solution: The multiplier has powers \(0\) and \(-2\). The pairs reaching power \(1\) are \((1,0)\) and \((3,-2)\).
In \((1+x)^5\), the \(x\) coefficient is \(5\), and the \(x^3\) coefficient is \(10\).
The coefficient is \(-5\). Stopping the first expansion at \(x\) would miss the contribution from \(x^3\). The original domain remains \(x\ne0\).

examples.title: See which powers cancel when the signs change
examples.question: Find the nonzero terms of \((1+x)^5+(1-x)^5\) and \((1+x)^5-(1-x)^5\).
solution:
Adding cancels each odd-power pair and doubles each even-power pair:

\[(1+x)^5+(1-x)^5=2+20x^2+10x^4.\]

Subtracting cancels each even-power pair and doubles each odd-power pair:

\[(1+x)^5-(1-x)^5=10x+20x^3+2x^5.\]

examples.title: Use a difference of squares before expanding
examples.question: Find the coefficient of \(x^4\) in \((1+x)^4(1-x)^4\).
solution:
The desired contribution uses the square of \(-x^2\):

\[\binom{4}{2}(-x^2)^2=6x^4.\]

The coefficient is \(6\). The full expression has only even powers:

\[(1-x^2)^4=1-4x^2+6x^4-4x^6+x^8.\]

examples.title: Unequal outer powers leave an extra factor
examples.question: Find the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \((1+x)^5(1-x)^3\).
solution:
Pair three copies of each opposite-sign bracket. Two copies of \(1+x\) remain:

\[(1+x)^5(1-x)^3=(1-x^2)^3(1+x)^2.\]
The first factor has only even powers. The only pair producing \(x^3\) is its \(-3x^2\) multiplied by the second factor’s \(2x\).
The coefficient is \(-6\). Unequal outer powers need not give an expression containing only even powers.

extraPractice.title: Include both routes to the target power
extraPractice.prompt: Find the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \((2+x)(1-x)^5\). Show the contributions before adding them.

retry.feedback: You have counted the constant times the cubic term. Also include \(x\) times the quadratic term.

extraPractice.hint: The constant \(2\) multiplies the cubic term; \(x\) multiplies the quadratic term.

extraPractice.title: Include all three contribution pairs
extraPractice.prompt: Find the coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1-3x+2x^2)(1+2x)^4\).
extraPractice.hint: Pair powers \((0,2)\), \((1,1)\) and \((2,0)\). Keep each multiplier sign.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The needed coefficients in the second factor are \(1,8,24\), from

    \[(1+2x)^4=1+8x+24x^2+32x^3+16x^4.\]
  2. \[[x^2]\bigl((1-3x+2x^2)(1+2x)^4\bigr)=1(24)-3(8)+2(1)=2.\]

extraPractice.title: A missing odd power can be supplied by another factor
extraPractice.prompt: Find the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \((1+x^2)^4(1-2x)\). Also give the exponent of the term selected from \((1+x^2)^4\) for the nonzero contribution.

retry.feedback: The first factor has no cubic term, but its \(x^2\) term combines with \(-2x\).

fields.label: Selected exponent from the first factor

extraPractice.hint: The first factor has only even powers. The \(-2x\) term can turn a quadratic term into a cubic term.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[(1+x^2)^4=1+4x^2+6x^4+4x^6+x^8.\]

  2. The contribution from the constant in the second factor is zero. The other contribution is

    \[(4x^2)(-2x)=-8x^3.\]

  3. The requested coefficient is \(-8\), and the selected exponent from the first factor is \(2\).

extraPractice.title: Use a difference of squares before expanding
extraPractice.prompt: Find the coefficients of \(x^4\) and \(x^3\) in \((1+x)^3(1-x)^3\).
extraPractice.hint: Both factors have the same outer power. Combine the brackets first.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[(1+x)^3(1-x)^3=\bigl((1+x)(1-x)\bigr)^3=(1-x^2)^3.\]
  2. \[(1-x^2)^3=1-3x^2+3x^4-x^6.\]

  3. The coefficients are \(3\) and \(0\). Every surviving exponent is even.

extraPractice.title: Account for an outside power first
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x\ne0\), find the coefficient of \(x^2\) in \(\frac{(1+3x)^4(1-x)}{x}\).

fields.label: Required exponent in the two-bracket product

extraPractice.hint: The outside \(x^{-1}\) shifts every exponent down by one. Find the cubic coefficient of the numerator.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Inside the numerator, target exponent \(2+1=3\). Stopping at the quadratic terms would lose a required contribution.

    \[(1+3x)^4=1+12x+54x^2+108x^3+81x^4.\]
  2. \[[x^3]\bigl((1+3x)^4(1-x)\bigr)=108-54=54.\]

  3. Dividing by \(x\) changes \(54x^3\) to \(54x^2\); it does not change the coefficient. The original domain remains \(x\ne0\).

extraPractice.title: Include negative powers in the exponent search
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x\ne0\), find the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \(\left(x^2+\frac{1}{x}\right)^4(1-2x)\). State the domain of the original expression.

retry.feedback: Include the coefficient \(-2\) from the second factor.

extraPractice.hint: In the first factor the exponents are \(8-3r\), with \(r=0,1,2,3,4\). Look for exponents \(3\) and \(2\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\left(x^2+\frac{1}{x}\right)^4=x^8+4x^5+6x^2+4x^{-1}+x^{-4}.\]

  2. There is no \(x^3\) term in the first factor. The other route is

    \[(6x^2)(-2x)=-12x^3.\]

  3. The coefficient is \(-12\). Negative integer powers are defined for negative values too, but \(x=0\) remains excluded.

starters.title: A cancellation determines the multiplier
starters.question:
The coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+kx)(1-2x)^5\) is zero, where \(k\) is real.

Find \(k\), then find the coefficient of \(x^3\) in the same product. Show the contributing pairs.
starters.hint: The needed coefficients of \((1-2x)^5\) are \(1,-10,40,-80\). Write the quadratic coefficient as a linear expression in \(k\).
starters.solution:
1. Through the cubic term, the binomial contributions are

    \[1+5(-2x)+10(-2x)^2+10(-2x)^3=1-10x+40x^2-80x^3.\]

  2. Higher terms do not affect the requested coefficients. For the quadratic coefficient,

    \[40-10k=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=4.\]

  3. The cubic coefficient is

    \[-80+40k=-80+160=80.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: Form the quadratic coefficient \(40-10k\) using both pairs.
  • 1 mark: Solve to obtain \(k=4\).
  • 1 mark: Form the cubic coefficient \(-80+40k\).
  • 1 mark: Evaluate the requested coefficient as \(80\).

starters.title: Use parity, then check a cancellation
starters.question:
Let \(F(x)=(1+x)^6+(1-x)^6\) and \(G(x)=(1-x^2)F(x)\).

Explain on paper why \(G\) has no odd-power terms. Find its coefficients of \(x^2\), \(x^4\) and \(x^6\).
starters.hint: Odd powers have opposite signs in the two expansions defining \(F\); even powers add. Multiplication by \(x^2\) preserves whether an exponent is even.
starters.solution:
1. \[F(x)=2+30x^2+30x^4+2x^6.\]

  2. The odd contributions cancel in \(F\). Both exponents in the multiplier are even, so every exponent in \(G\) is also even.

  3. \[[x^2]G=30-2=28,\qquad [x^4]G=30-30=0.\]
  4. \[[x^6]G=2-30=-28.\]

  5. As a full check,

    \[G(x)=2+28x^2-28x^6-2x^8.\]

    The quadratic and sextic coefficients have opposite signs; the quartic term cancels completely.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: Explain cancellation of the odd powers in the sum defining the first polynomial.
  • 1 mark: Obtain \(F(x)=2+30x^2+30x^4+2x^6\).
  • 1 mark: Calculate the quadratic coefficient \(28\).
  • 1 mark: Include both quartic contributions to obtain \(0\).
  • 1 mark: Calculate the sextic coefficient \(-28\).
  • 1 mark: Explain that multiplication by an even-power polynomial preserves the absence of odd powers.

starters.title: Two binomials contribute several routes
starters.question: Find the coefficients of \(x^3\) and \(x^4\) in \((1+2x)^3(1-x)^4\). Write the exponent pairs used for each coefficient.
starters.hint: Make two short coefficient rows, with an entry for every power. For a target exponent, multiply entries whose exponents add to that target.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: Obtain the first complete coefficient row.
  • 1 mark: Obtain the required coefficients of the second factor, retaining signs.
  • 1 mark: Include all four cubic contribution pairs.
  • 1 mark: Obtain the cubic coefficient \(-8\).
  • 1 mark: Include all four quartic contribution pairs, without inventing a fourth-degree term in the cubic factor.
  • 1 mark: Obtain the quartic coefficient \(17\).

revision.body:
Choose the target power, list the pairs, multiply their coefficients, then add.

Match exponents

\[(a_ix^i)(b_jx^j)=a_i b_jx^{i+j}.\]

For \(x^m\), use all available pairs \(i+j=m\). Missing powers have coefficient \(0\). Include constant contributions from both ends. Cancellation can also make the final coefficient zero.

Common multipliers

Let \(C_j\) be the coefficient of \(x^j\) in \(F\).

\[[x^m]\bigl((a+bx)F\bigr)=aC_m+bC_{m-1}.\]\[[x^m]\bigl((a+bx+cx^2)F\bigr)=aC_m+bC_{m-1}+cC_{m-2}.\]

An outside \(x^k\) changes the target in \(F\) to \(m-k\).

Keep enough terms

For nonnegative powers only, ignore terms above the target degree. With negative powers, list pairs first: \(x^3\cdot x^{-2}=x\). Preserve original domain restrictions.

Two binomial factors: obtain each required coefficient, then sum all target-producing products. A selected coefficient can be exact even when the lists are truncated.

Derive the odd-and-even shortcuts

\(F(x)+F(-x)\): odd powers cancel; even coefficients double. \(F(x)-F(-x)\): even powers cancel; odd coefficients double.

\[(a+b)^n(a-b)^n=(a^2-b^2)^n.\]

Thus \((1+cx)^n(1-cx)^n\) has only even powers. With unequal outer powers, keep the leftover factor.
revision.checks:
• All pairs reach the requested exponent?
  • Signs and constant contributions included?
  • Missing powers kept as zeros?
  • Truncation and any symmetry shortcut justified?

orig_binomial_expansion_parameters.description: Turn coefficient information into equations, retain every possible branch, and check that each solution satisfies the original algebra and the stated restrictions.

sections.title: How does a coefficient reveal an unknown constant?
sections.label: Build the coefficient equation
sections.intro: Start by selecting the required power. Write its complete coefficient in terms of the unknown, then equate it to the value given in the question. The unknown can appear in either term of the bracket. We write \(C_r=[x^r]F(x)\) for the coefficient of \(x^r\) in an expression \(F(x)\).

blocks.html:
For \((a+bx)^n\), with positive integer \(n\) and \(0\le r\le n\), the \(x^r\) contribution is

\[\binom{n}{r}a^{n-r}b^r x^r.\]

Include the power of the first constant as well as the scale on \(x\). A coefficient equation concerns the numerical part only.

blocks.title: Keep both square-root branches
blocks.prompt: The coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((3+bx)^4\) is \(216\). Find all real values of \(b\).
blocks.hint: The coefficient is \(\binom{4}{2}3^2b^2\), not just \(6b^2\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[\binom{4}{2}3^2b^2=216\Longrightarrow54b^2=216\Longrightarrow b^2=4.\]
  2. \[b=-2\text{ or }b=2.\]

  3. Both values produce coefficient \(216\). No sign restriction was given.

blocks.html: If \(a^2=c>0\), both \(a=\sqrt{c}\) and \(a=-\sqrt{c}\) are candidates. Keep them until the question’s sign or domain conditions select a branch.

If the first constant in a bracket is zero, simplify the bracket directly. For example, \((0+bx)^n=b^nx^n\). Lower coefficients then vanish; do not use a formula requiring division by that first constant.

sections.title: Which solutions can division accidentally remove?
sections.label: Zero cases and ratios
sections.intro: An equality such as \(C_2=C_1\) or \(C_2=3C_1\) can hold when both coefficients are zero. Move all terms to one side and factor before cancelling a parameter that might be zero.

blocks.html:
1. In \((1+ax)^5\), the coefficients of \(x\) and \(x^2\) are \(5a\) and \(10a^2\).
  2. Set them equal and factor before dividing.\[10a^2=5a\implies5a(2a-1)=0.\]
  3. At \(a=0\), both coefficients are zero. At \(a=\frac12\), both are \(\frac52\). Both satisfy the given condition.

The equation \(10a^2=5a\) has two branches: \(a=0\) and \(a=\frac{1}{2}\). Dividing by \(a\) would discard the first branch.

blocks.title: A coefficient equality may allow zero
blocks.prompt: In \((1+kx)^4\), the coefficients of \(x\) and \(x^2\) are equal. Find all real values of \(k\).
blocks.hint: Write \(4k=6k^2\), then factor without dividing by \(k\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[4k=6k^2\Longrightarrow2k(3k-2)=0.\]
  2. \[k=0\text{ or }k=\frac{2}{3}.\]

  3. At \(k=0\), both coefficients are zero. At \(k=\frac{2}{3}\), both are \(\frac{8}{3}\).

blocks.html: An equality of coefficients and a ratio condition are different. The equation \(C_2=C_1\) may permit both zero. The statement \(\frac{C_2}{C_1}=1\) requires \(C_1\ne0\) before any algebra.
Likewise, a parameter in a denominator is restricted from the start. A bracket containing \(\frac{x}{k}\) requires \(k\ne0\), even if a later multiplied equation happens to produce \(k=0\).
Write “if this factor is zero” and check that case before dividing. If the question already says the parameter or denominator is nonzero, state that restriction and then simplify.

sections.title: How do I find an unknown outer power?
sections.label: Integer exponents and boundaries
sections.intro: The finite binomial theorem here uses a positive integer outer power. An algebraic root is only a candidate: it must also satisfy that integer condition. A nonzero \(x^r\) coefficient requires \(n\ge r\).

blocks.title: The outer power must be a positive integer
blocks.prompt: The coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+x)^n\) is \(36\), where \(n\) is a positive integer. Find \(n\).
blocks.hint: A nonzero quadratic coefficient requires \(n\ge2\). Solve \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}=36\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[n(n-1)=72\Longrightarrow n^2-n-72=(n-9)(n+8)=0.\]

  2. The candidates are \(9\) and \(-8\). Only the positive integer \(n=9\) is allowed, and \(\binom{9}{2}=36\).

blocks.html: If \(n<r\), the coefficient of \(x^r\) in \((a+bx)^n\) is \(0\). When comparing coefficients and the question does not require them to be nonzero, inspect these small-power cases before dividing factorial expressions.
Do not put a negative integer into a factorial formula such as \((n-r)!\). For indices beyond the finite expansion, read the coefficient as zero from the polynomial itself.

sections.title: How do two coefficients determine linked unknowns?
sections.label: Ratios and simultaneous equations
sections.intro: Label the needed coefficients first, then write one equation for each condition. If a known coefficient is nonzero, a ratio can remove common factors. Otherwise use substitution or elimination while keeping zero cases.

blocks.html:
For \((1+ax)^n\), with \(n\ge2\),

\[C_1=na,\qquad C_2=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}a^2.\]

When \(C_1\ne0\), their ratio is

\[\frac{C_2}{C_1}=\frac{(n-1)a}{2}.\]

This ratio is a consequence of the coefficient formulas, not a replacement for checking its denominator.

blocks.title: Two coefficients determine the scale and exponent
blocks.prompt: In \((1+px)^n\), the coefficients of \(x\) and \(x^2\) are \(8\) and \(28\), respectively. Here \(n\) is a positive integer. Find \(n\) and \(p\).
blocks.hint: Use \(np=8\). Since the linear coefficient is nonzero, divide the quadratic coefficient equation by the linear one.
blocks.solution:
1. \[np=8,\qquad\frac{n(n-1)}{2}p^2=28.\]
  2. \[\frac{(n-1)p}{2}=\frac{28}{8}=\frac{7}{2}\Longrightarrow(n-1)p=7.\]

  3. Subtracting this from \(np=8\) gives \(p=1\). Thus \(n=8\).

  4. \[8(1)=8,\qquad\binom{8}{2}(1)^2=28.\]

blocks.html:
For \((1+ax)^n\) with first coefficient \(C_1=6\), the positive integer exponent obeys

\[na=6,\qquad a=\frac6n,\qquad C_2=\frac{n(n-1)}2a^2=\frac{18(n-1)}n.\]
GivenEquationDecision
\(C_2=15\)\(18(n-1)=15n\)Accept \(n=6,\ a=1\).
\(C_2=14\)\(18(n-1)=14n\)Reject \(n=\frac92\) because it is not an integer.

With \(C_1=6\), the condition \(C_2=15\) gives \((n,a)=(6,1)\). Changing \(C_2\) to \(14\) gives the inadmissible noninteger candidate \(n=\frac{9}{2}\).
For a product, extract each coefficient by matching exponent pairs, then solve the resulting simultaneous equations. Keep each second parameter paired with the first parameter value that produced it.

blocks.title: Keep simultaneous solutions in their correct pairs
blocks.prompt: The coefficients of \(x\) and \(x^2\) in \((1+ax)^2(1+bx)\) are \(5\) and \(8\), respectively. Find every ordered pair \((a,b)\).
blocks.hint: The coefficient equations are \(2a+b=5\) and \(a^2+2ab=8\). Substitute \(b=5-2a\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[a^2+2a(5-2a)=8\Longrightarrow3a^2-10a+8=0.\]
  2. \[(3a-4)(a-2)=0\Longrightarrow a=\frac{4}{3}\text{ or }a=2.\]
  3. \[a=\frac{4}{3}\Longrightarrow b=\frac{7}{3},\qquad a=2\Longrightarrow b=1.\]

  4. For \((2,1)\), the coefficients are \(4+1=5\) and \(4+4=8\). For \(\left(\frac{4}{3},\frac{7}{3}\right)\), they are \(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{7}{3}=5\) and \(\frac{16}{9}+\frac{56}{9}=8\).

blocks.html: Two possible values of \(a\) and two of \(b\) do not automatically give four solutions. Report the ordered pairs that satisfy both original equations.

sections.title: How do I decide which candidates really work?
sections.label: Admissibility and impossibility
sections.intro: Finish by checking every original condition: integer outer power, allowed parameter signs, nonzero denominators and each stated coefficient relation. Use an unused sign or coefficient condition to select among branches.

blocks.title: An impossible coefficient is a valid conclusion
blocks.prompt: The coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((2+tx)^4\) is claimed to be \(-24\). Find all real values of \(t\), or enter “no solutions”.
blocks.hint: Write the coefficient as a positive constant times \(t^2\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[\binom{4}{2}2^2t^2=24t^2.\]
  2. \[24t^2=-24\Longrightarrow t^2=-1.\]

  3. A real square cannot be negative, so no real parameter satisfies the condition.

blocks.html: “No solution” may be the correct conclusion. A required real square may be negative; an outer power may be noninteger; or the candidate pairs may fail one of the original conditions. Explain the specific obstruction.

When coefficients are given numerically, substituting a candidate into their original formulas is usually quicker than expanding the whole polynomial. Check both equations in a linked problem, not only the one used last.
Keep exact fractions and roots while solving. Rounding a candidate outer power to a nearby integer does not make it admissible. If a parameter is restricted, show why any rejected candidate fails.

glossary.definition: A constant whose value is to be found or restricted.
A value produced by algebra that still needs checking against the original conditions.
One possible case, such as a positive or negative root or a zero factor.
Satisfying every stated condition and original domain restriction.
One coefficient divided by another, requiring the denominator coefficient to be nonzero.
Two parameter values recorded together in a specified order.

examples.title: Turn the complete coefficient into an equation
examples.question: The coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((2+ax)^4\) is \(216\). Find all real values of \(a\).
solution: Both give \(24(9)=216\). A positive coefficient does not force the parameter to be positive when the parameter is squared.

examples.title: Factor before cancelling a parameter
examples.question: In \((1+ax)^5\), the coefficients of \(x^2\) and \(x\) are equal. Find all real values of \(a\).
solution: At \(a=0\), both coefficients are \(0\). At \(a=\frac{1}{2}\), both are \(\frac{5}{2}\). Dividing by \(a\) at the start would lose the zero solution.

examples.title: Solve for an integer outer power
examples.question: The coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+x)^n\) is \(45\). Find the positive integer \(n\).
solution: The candidates are \(10\) and \(-9\). The allowed value is \(n=10\), and \(\binom{10}{2}=45\).

examples.title: A missing-coefficient boundary can satisfy an equality
examples.question: In \((1+x)^n\), the coefficient of \(x^3\) equals twice the coefficient of \(x^2\). Find all positive integers \(n\).
solution: Check small powers before dividing coefficients. At \(n=1\), both requested coefficients are \(0\), so the equality holds. At \(n=2\), they are \(0\) and \(1\), so it fails.

For \(n\ge3\), the quadratic coefficient is nonzero, so division is valid:

\[\frac{\binom{n}{3}}{\binom{n}{2}}=\frac{n-2}{3}=2.\]
At \(n=8\), the coefficients are \(56\) and \(28\). Thus all allowed values are \(n=1\) and \(n=8\).

examples.title: Use a ratio only after its denominator is known to be nonzero
examples.question: In \((1+ax)^n\), the coefficients of \(x\) and \(x^2\) are \(6\) and \(15\), respectively. Find the positive integer \(n\) and the real constant \(a\).
solution:
The first coefficient is \(6\), so division by it is safe:

\[\frac{(n-1)a}{2}=\frac{15}{6}=\frac{5}{2}\Longrightarrow(n-1)a=5.\]

examples.title: Two product coefficients give paired parameter values
examples.question: In \((1+ax)^3(1+bx)\), the coefficients of \(x\) and \(x^2\) are \(5\) and \(6\), respectively. Find all ordered pairs \((a,b)\).
solution: Check each complete pair. For \(\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{7}{2}\right)\), the coefficients are \(5\) and \(\frac{3}{4}+\frac{21}{4}=6\). For \((2,-1)\), they are \(6-1=5\) and \(12-6=6\). Both pairs work.

examples.title: Use an extra sign condition to select a branch
examples.question: The constant coefficient of \((a+x)^4\) is \(81\), and its linear coefficient is negative. Find \(a\).
solution: For \(a=3\), this is \(108>0\). For \(a=-3\), it is \(-108<0\). The required value is \(a=-3\).

examples.title: A real solution may fail the integer condition
examples.question: Could \((1+ax)^n\), with \(n\) a positive integer, have linear coefficient \(6\) and quadratic coefficient \(14\)?
solution: This is not an integer. The algebraic candidate is inadmissible, so no positive-integer finite binomial expansion has both stated coefficients.
