extraPractice.title: Keep both signs until another condition chooses one
extraPractice.prompt: In \((1+ax)^5\), the coefficient of \(x^2\) is \(90\), where \(a\) is real. Find all possible values of \(a\). For the positive value, find the coefficient of \(x^3\).
extraPractice.hint: The quadratic coefficient is \(\binom{5}{2}a^2\). Taking a square root gives two candidates.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[10a^2=90\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a^2=9\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=\pm3.\]

  2. Both signs give quadratic coefficient \(90\). With \(a=3\),

    \[[x^3](1+3x)^5=\binom{5}{3}3^3=270.\]

extraPractice.title: Do not divide away an allowed zero
extraPractice.prompt: The coefficients of \(x\) and \(x^2\) in \((2+kx)^4\) are equal. Find all real values of \(k\), and the common coefficient for the nonzero value.

retry.feedback: Check \(k=0\) in the original bracket before cancelling \(k\).

fields.label: Common coefficient for the nonzero value

extraPractice.hint: Write the coefficients as \(32k\) and \(24k^2\), then factor their difference.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[32k=24k^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad8k(3k-4)=0.\]
  2. \[k=0\quad\text{or}\quad k=\frac{4}{3}.\]

  3. When \(k=0\), the whole expression is \(16\), so both requested coefficients are zero. This satisfies the condition.

  4. For the other value,

    \[32\cdot\frac{4}{3}=\frac{128}{3}=24\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^2.\]

extraPractice.title: An algebraic root may not be a valid exponent
extraPractice.prompt: The coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+x)^n\) is \(28\), where \(n\) is a positive integer. Find \(n\), then the coefficient of \(x^3\).
extraPractice.hint: A nonzero quadratic coefficient requires \(n\ge2\). Use \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}=28\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[n^2-n-56=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(n-8)(n+7)=0.\]

  2. The algebraic candidates are \(8\) and \(-7\). Only \(n=8\) is a positive integer.

  3. \[[x^3](1+x)^8=\binom{8}{3}=56.\]

extraPractice.title: Two coefficients determine two unknowns
extraPractice.prompt: In \((1+px)^n\), the coefficients of \(x\) and \(x^2\) are \(12\) and \(60\), respectively. Here \(n\) is a positive integer and \(p\) is real. Find \(n\), \(p\) and the coefficient of \(x^3\).
extraPractice.hint: Use \(np=12\) to write \(p=\frac{12}{n}\), then substitute into the quadratic coefficient. The nonzero data justify the required divisions.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[np=12,\qquad \frac{n(n-1)}{2}p^2=60.\]

  2. The quadratic coefficient is nonzero, so \(n\ge2\); also \(p\ne0\). Substitution gives

    \[72\frac{n-1}{n}=60.\]
  3. \[72n-72=60n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=6,\qquad p=2.\]

  4. Check: \(6(2)=12\) and \(15(2^2)=60\). The cubic coefficient is

    \[\binom{6}{3}2^3=160.\]

extraPractice.title: Use both original conditions
extraPractice.prompt: The constant term in \((a+x)^4\) is \(16\), and the coefficient of \(x\) is \(32\). Find all real values of \(a\), then the coefficient of \(x^2\).
extraPractice.hint: The first condition allows two signs. Test them in the linear coefficient \(4a^3\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[a^4=16\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=2\ \text{or}\ a=-2.\]

  2. The linear condition is \(4a^3=32\). It holds for \(a=2\); \(a=-2\) gives \(-32\), so it is rejected.

  3. \[[x^2](2+x)^4=\binom{4}{2}2^2=24.\]

extraPractice.title: Recognise impossible coefficient data
extraPractice.prompt: Find all real values of \(b\) for which the coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+bx)^3\) is \(-6\). If there are none, enter “no solutions”.
extraPractice.hint: The quadratic coefficient is \(3b^2\). What sign can this have when \(b\) is real?
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[3b^2=-6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b^2=-2.\]

  2. A real square is nonnegative. There are no real values satisfying the coefficient condition.

starters.title: Small exponents can create an extra case
starters.question:
For a positive integer \(n\), the coefficient of \(x^3\) in \((1+2x)^n\) is twice the coefficient of \(x^2\). A power that does not occur has coefficient zero.

Find every possible \(n\). For the larger value, find the coefficient of \(x^4\).
starters.hint: Check \(n=1\) and \(n=2\) directly. Then use the coefficient formulas for \(n\ge3\), where cancelling their nonzero factors is valid.
starters.solution:
1. For \(n=1\), both coefficients are zero, so the condition holds. For \(n=2\), they are \(0\) and \(4\); \(0\ne2(4)\), so this value fails.

  2. For \(n\ge3\),

    \[8\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}=2\left(4\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\right).\]

  3. Divide by the nonzero common factor \(4n(n-1)\):

    \[\frac{n-2}{3}=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=5.\]

  4. At \(n=5\), the coefficients are \(80\) and \(40\), so the relation holds. The complete set is \(\{1,5\}\).

  5. \[[x^4](1+2x)^5=\binom{5}{4}2^4=80.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: check the small-exponent cases and retain the valid value \(n=1\).
  • 1 mark: form the cubic and quadratic coefficient equation for \(n\ge3\).
  • 1 mark: simplify using a justified nonzero common factor.
  • 1 mark: obtain \(n=5\) and give the complete set.
  • 1 mark: verify the coefficient relation for the nontrivial value.
  • 1 mark: obtain the quartic coefficient \(80\).

starters.title: Retain matched pairs of coupled parameters
starters.question: In \((1+ax)^4(1+bx)^2\), the coefficients of \(x\) and \(x^2\) are \(2\) and \(-1\), respectively. Find all real pairs \((a,b)\). For the pair with \(a>0\), find the coefficient of \(x^3\).
starters.hint: The linear coefficient is \(4a+2b\). The quadratic coefficient has three contributions: \(6a^2+8ab+b^2\).
starters.solution:
1. \[4a+2b=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b=1-2a.\]
  2. \[6a^2+8ab+b^2=-1.\]

  3. Substitute the expression for \(b\):

    \[-6a^2+4a+1=-1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(3a+1)(a-1)=0.\]

  4. Reconstruct the matched values:

    \[(a,b)=(1,-1)\quad\text{or}\quad\left(-\frac{1}{3},\frac{5}{3}\right).\]

  5. Both pairs satisfy the original equations. For the fractional pair, the linear coefficient is \(-\frac{4}{3}+\frac{10}{3}=2\), and the quadratic coefficient is \(\frac{6-40+25}{9}=-1\).

  6. For \(a=1,b=-1\), the cubic coefficient is

    \[4a^3+12a^2b+4ab^2=4-12+4=-4.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: form the linear relation and express one parameter in terms of the other.
  • 1 mark: include all three quadratic coefficient contributions.
  • 1 mark: obtain and factor the quadratic equation for the first parameter.
  • 2 marks: give both correctly paired parameter values and verify them in the original conditions.
  • 1 mark: obtain the cubic coefficient \(-4\) for the positive first parameter.

starters.title: A later coefficient selects one sign
starters.question:
For \(x\ne0\), the constant term in \(\left(kx^2-\frac{1}{x}\right)^6\) is \(135\), and its coefficient of \(x^3\) is negative.

Find all real candidates from the constant-term condition, determine the value of \(k\) satisfying both conditions, and find the coefficient of \(x^6\).
starters.hint: The exponent of \(x\) is \(12-3r\). The constant term uses \(r=4\); the cubic term uses \(r=3\), so its dependence on \(k\) has an odd power.
starters.solution:
1. \[T_{r+1}=\binom{6}{r}k^{6-r}(-1)^r x^{12-3r}.\]

  2. For the constant term, \(r=4\), so

    \[15k^2=135\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=\pm3.\]

  3. The cubic coefficient, at \(r=3\), is \(-20k^3\). It is \(-540\) when \(k=3\), but \(540\) when \(k=-3\). The negative-coefficient condition selects \(k=3\).

  4. For \(x^6\), solve \(12-3r=6\), giving \(r=2\):

    \[\binom{6}{2}3^4(-1)^2=15(81)=1215.\]

  5. The original restriction \(x\ne0\) remains in force.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: derive the correct exponent and select the constant-term index.
  • 1 mark: form \(15k^2=135\).
  • 1 mark: retain both candidates \(k=\pm3\).
  • 1 mark: derive the cubic coefficient \(-20k^3\).
  • 1 mark: use its sign to select \(k=3\).
  • 1 mark: select the sextic index and obtain coefficient \(1215\).

revision.body:
Extract, equate, solve all cases, then check the original conditions.

Coefficient equation

\[[x^r](a+bx)^n=\binom{n}{r}a^{n-r}b^r\qquad(0\le r\le n).\]

Include both constants. If a bracket constant is zero, simplify the bracket directly. Even powers can give positive and negative parameter branches.

Zero and denominator cases

Factor before dividing by a parameter. \(C_2=C_1\) may allow both coefficients to be zero; \(\frac{C_2}{C_1}=1\) requires \(C_1\ne0\). A parameter in an original denominator must stay nonzero.

Unknown integer power

Require positive integer \(n\). A nonzero \(x^r\) coefficient needs \(n\ge r\). For \(n<r\), the coefficient is zero: check small-power boundaries before cancelling.

For \((1+ax)^n\), \(n\ge2\):

\[C_1=na,\qquad C_2=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}a^2.\]\[\frac{C_2}{C_1}=\frac{(n-1)a}{2}\qquad(C_1\ne0).\]

Linked parameters and final checks

For products, sum every contribution to each coefficient. Solve the resulting simultaneous equations and preserve ordered pairs. Check every pair in both original equations.

Reject only for a stated reason: a forbidden sign, zero denominator, noninteger exponent, inconsistent coefficient or impossible real square. Never round an exponent into an allowed integer.
revision.checks:
• Complete coefficient expressions?
  • Zero and both sign branches considered?
  • Positive integer exponent and original domains checked?
  • Every paired solution checked in every original condition?
revision.examTip: Every paired solution checked in every original condition?

orig_binomial_expansion_approximations.description: Match the numerical input, calculate what the truncated expansion leaves out, and use exact bounds and parameter restrictions to justify the final answer.

sections.title: Which value belongs in the expansion?
sections.label: Match the numerical input
sections.intro: A short binomial expansion estimates a numerical power by retaining only the requested terms. First equate the bracket’s base to the number you need. If the bracket is \(1+cx\), solve \(1+cx=\text{target base}\); do not substitute the target itself for \(x\).

blocks.html:
For a positive integer \(n\), the quadratic truncation of \((1+x)^n\) is

\[Q_2(x)=1+nx+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}x^2.\]

Use this as an approximation when omitted terms remain. Their size, not the length of the formula, decides its accuracy.

blocks.title: Match the target base before substituting
blocks.prompt: Use the terms through \(t^2\) in \((1+3t)^4\) to approximate \(1.06^4\). Give the required value of \(t\) and the exact value of the retained polynomial.
blocks.hint: Solve \(1+3t=1.06\). The retained polynomial is \(1+12t+54t^2\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[3t=0.06\Longrightarrow t=0.02=\frac{1}{50}.\]
  2. \[1+12(0.02)+54(0.02)^2=1+0.24+0.0216=1.2616.\]

  3. Thus \(1.06^4\approx1.2616\) using the specified terms. This is the exact value of the shorter polynomial, not the exact value of the original fourth power.

blocks.html:
If you factor the base, raise the outside factor to the outer power. For \(a\ne0\),

\[(a+h)^n=a^n\left(1+\frac{h}{a}\right)^n.\]

The retained polynomial and its remainder are both multiplied by \(a^n\).

sections.title: How far is the approximation from the true value?
sections.label: The exact finite remainder
sections.intro: Let \(P\) be the full finite expansion and \(Q_j\) its terms through degree \(j\). Define the signed remainder by \(R_j=P-Q_j\). It is exactly the sum of the omitted terms.

blocks.html:
\[P(x)=Q_j(x)+R_j(x).\]

Positive \(R_j\): the approximation is below the true value. Negative \(R_j\): it is above. Absolute error is \(|R_j|\).

\[\text{Relative error}=\frac{|R_j|}{|P|},\qquad\text{percentage error}=100\frac{|R_j|}{|P|}\%.\]

Relative and percentage errors require \(P\ne0\).

For \(F(x)=(1+x)^6\) and \(Q_2(x)=1+6x+15x^2\), subtract the retained terms.

\[R(x)=F(x)-Q_2(x)=20x^3+15x^4+6x^5+x^6.\]

At \(x=0.04\), \(Q_2=1.264\) and \(F=1.265319018496\). The error \(R=0.001319018496\) is positive, so the approximation is an underestimate. For small negative inputs the error has the opposite sign.

At \(x=0.04\), the quadratic value for \((1+x)^6\) is \(1.264\); the exact value is \(1.265319018496\). The omitted polynomial gives their positive difference \(0.001319018496\).

blocks.title: Read the sign of the exact remainder
blocks.prompt: Let \(P(x)=(1+x)^3\), approximated by \(Q(x)=1+3x\). At \(x=-0.05\), find the signed remainder \(R=P-Q\). Is \(Q\) an underestimate or an overestimate?
blocks.hint: The exact remainder is \(R(x)=3x^2+x^3\). A positive \(P-Q\) means the true value is larger.

blocks.html: A positive-integer binomial expansion is a finite identity on its original domain. It has no convergence restriction such as \(|x|<1\). A truncation can still be a poor approximation; check its actual remainder or a justified bound.

sections.title: Can I guarantee an error or a rounded answer?
sections.label: Bounds, degree and rounding
sections.intro:
For a whole input interval, bound each omitted term. If \(R(x)=\sum c_rx^r\) has positive integer powers and \(|x|\le h\), the triangle inequality gives

\[|R(x)|\le\sum |c_r|h^r.\]

This bound allows for all omitted terms, including mixed signs. On \(0\le x\le h\), nonnegative coefficients also tell you \(R\ge0\).

blocks.title: Bound every omitted term on the interval
blocks.prompt: Approximate \((1+x)^4\) by \(Q(x)=1+4x+6x^2\) for \(0\le x\le0.02\). Find the largest absolute error on this interval and state whether \(Q\le(1+x)^4\) throughout it.

fields.label: Is the retained polynomial at most the true value?

blocks.hint: The remainder is \(4x^3+x^4\). Each omitted term is nonnegative and increases as \(x\) increases on this interval.
blocks.solution:
1. \[0\le R(x)=4x^3+x^4\le4(0.02)^3+(0.02)^4=0.00003216.\]

  2. The upper value is attained at \(x=0.02\), so it is the largest absolute error. Also \(R\ge0\), hence \(Q\le(1+x)^4\).

blocks.html: To justify rounding, turn the remainder bound into an interval for the true value. Every value in that interval must round to the same result. Check the nearby midpoints between rounded values.

To prove a truncation is the least sufficient one, show that it meets the strict error requirement and that all shorter choices fail. With positive omitted terms at a positive input, shorter truncations have larger errors. With mixed signs, compare the actual remainders; do not assume every added term reduces the absolute error.

sections.title: How many inner terms survive a division or cancellation?
sections.label: Plan the expansion depth
sections.intro: Plan backward from the final power. Multiplication by \(x^{-s}\) lowers each exponent by \(s\). To retain terms through degree \(j\) after that shift, the inner expansion may need terms through degree \(j+s\).

blocks.html: Subtracting matching low-degree terms can remove the apparent beginning of an expansion. Expand far enough first, perform the subtraction, then shift powers and identify the final remainder.

blocks.title: A denominator determines how far to expand first
blocks.prompt: For \(x\ne0\), simplify \(F(x)=\frac{(1+3x)^3-1-9x}{x^2}\). Find its constant and linear coefficients. What degree must the numerator expansion reach to recover the linear term of \(F\)?
blocks.hint: Division by \(x^2\) lowers every exponent by two.
blocks.solution:
1. \[(1+3x)^3=1+9x+27x^2+27x^3.\]
  2. \[F(x)=\frac{27x^2+27x^3}{x^2}=27+27x\qquad(x\ne0).\]

  3. The numerator must include its cubic term. The simplified polynomial gives an extension at zero, but zero remains excluded from the original fraction.

blocks.html: Cancellation does not change the original domain. A fraction with denominator \(x^2\) still excludes \(x=0\), even if its simplified polynomial has a value there.

sections.title: What if a coefficient is itself a model with a parameter?
sections.label: Coupled coefficient models
sections.intro:
A coefficient extracted from a product may be a quadratic function of a parameter. First collect every contribution to the requested power. Then treat the resulting coefficient function as an algebra problem, preserving the parameter’s domain.

Write \([x^r]F(x)\) for the coefficient of \(x^r\) in \(F\). The input \(x\) used in the expansion and a model parameter such as \(k\) have different roles.

blocks.title: Keep an open parameter interval open
blocks.prompt:
Let \(C(k)\) be the coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+kx)^2(1+(2-k)x)^2\), where \(0<k<1\).

Find the lower and upper bounds of its range, state whether either is attained, and find the allowed \(k\) for which \(C(k)=5\).

options.upper: Only the upper bound is attained.

blocks.hint: Collect the three quadratic contributions and complete the square: \(C(k)=6-2(k-1)^2\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[C(k)=k^2+4k(2-k)+(2-k)^2=6-2(k-1)^2.\]

  2. For \(0<k<1\), we have \(0<(k-1)^2<1\). Hence \(4<C(k)<6\), with neither endpoint attained.

  3. \[6-2(k-1)^2=5\Longrightarrow k=1\pm\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\]

  4. Only \(k=1-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) belongs to \((0,1)\).

blocks.html: For a restricted range, complete the square and track the allowed square values. For a specified coefficient, solve for every parameter branch and check the original interval. Open endpoints are not attained unless another allowed input gives the same value.

For \(C(k)=6(k-1)^2-2\) with \(k>0\), count intersections only on the positive-parameter side.

LevelPositive solutions
\(m=-2\)A repeated solution at \(k=1\).
\(m=1\)Two solutions \(k=1\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\).
\(m=4\)Only \(k=2\) remains because \(k=0\) is excluded.

There are two distinct positive solutions exactly when \(-2

For \(C(k)=6(k-1)^2-2\), a horizontal level \(m\) meets the curve twice at positive \(k\) precisely when \(-2<m<4\). The lower boundary is a repeated root; at the upper boundary one root is zero.

blocks.title: Two positive roots need two strict conditions
blocks.prompt:
The coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+kx)^2(1+(k-3)x)^2\) is \(m\). Find the interval of \(m\) for which there are two distinct positive values of \(k\).

Enter its lower and upper bounds and choose the endpoint rule.
blocks.hint: The coefficient is \(6k^2-18k+9=6\left(k-\frac{3}{2}\right)^2-\frac{9}{2}\). Solve for both roots and require the smaller one to be positive.
blocks.solution:
1. \[k=\frac{3}{2}\pm\sqrt{\frac{2m+9}{12}}.\]

  2. Distinct real roots need \(2m+9>0\), so \(m>-\frac{9}{2}\).

  3. \[\frac{3}{2}-\sqrt{\frac{2m+9}{12}}>0\Longrightarrow\frac{2m+9}{12}<\frac{9}{4}\Longrightarrow m<9.\]
  4. \[-\frac{9}{2}<m<9.\]

  5. At the lower endpoint the roots coincide; at the upper endpoint one root is zero. Neither endpoint is allowed.

blocks.html: Translate each word into a separate condition. “Real” requires a nonnegative square-root input; “distinct” excludes a repeated root; “positive” excludes zero and negative roots. Check endpoints explicitly before writing the final interval.

glossary.definition: An expansion stopped after a specified degree or number of terms.
The true value minus the retained-polynomial value.
The nonnegative magnitude of the signed remainder.
Absolute error divided by the magnitude of the true value, when nonzero.
A justified upper limit on the absolute error over a specified set of inputs.
A midpoint separating values that round to neighbouring results.
A coefficient viewed as a function of a parameter.
A boundary value produced by at least one allowed input.

examples.title: Choose the increment and retain the requested terms
examples.question: Use the terms through \(x^2\) in \((1+x)^6\) to approximate \(1.04^6\).
solution: Therefore \(1.04^6\approx1.264\) using the specified quadratic approximation. Its exact error is found from the omitted terms below.

examples.title: Preserve the outside scale when the base is not near one
examples.question: Use a quadratic binomial approximation to estimate \(4.01^3\).
solution: The omitted contribution is \(64(0.0025)^3=0.000001\), so the exact value is \(64.481201\). The outside factor multiplies the error as well as the retained terms.

examples.title: Signed, absolute and percentage errors are different
examples.question: Approximate \((1+x)^6\) by \(Q_2(x)=1+6x+15x^2\). At \(x=-0.1\), find the signed remainder, absolute error and percentage error.
solution: The signed remainder is \(-0.018559\), so \(Q_2\) is an overestimate. The absolute error is \(0.018559\).
The percentage is rounded to three significant figures. Its denominator is the magnitude of the true value, not the approximation.

examples.title: Bound a whole interval by bounding every omitted term
examples.question: For \(0\le x\le0.04\), bound the error when \((1+x)^6\) is approximated by \(1+6x+15x^2\).
solution: Every term is nonnegative and increases as \(x\) increases on this interval. Replace each power by its value at \(0.04\):
The exact upper bound is reached at \(x=0.04\). Thus the quadratic approximation is at most the true value, and its absolute error is less than \(0.00132\) throughout the interval.

examples.title: Choose enough terms and check the rounding interval
examples.question: Approximate \(1.03^4\) using a truncation of \((1+x)^4\) at \(x=0.03\). Find the least retained degree that gives absolute error below \(10^{-4}\), and justify the correct answer to three decimal places.
solution: All contributions are positive at this input. Any earlier truncation omits still more positive terms, so it also fails the error requirement.
The least degree is \(3\), meaning four retained terms including the constant.
This whole interval lies between the rounding boundaries \(1.1255\) and \(1.1265\), so the correct three-decimal-place value is \(1.126\).

The quadratic value \(1.1254\) would round to \(1.125\), despite its error being below half a thousandth. The true value crosses the midpoint \(1.1255\); an error threshold alone does not guarantee the same rounding.

examples.title: Expand farther before dividing by a power
examples.question: For \(x\ne0\), find the terms through \(x^2\) in \(F(x)=\frac{(1+2x)^4-1-8x}{x^2}\). Use its linear truncation at \(x=0.01\) and find the exact omitted error.
solution: Division by \(x^2\) lowers powers by two, so the numerator must be expanded through degree four.
The exact value is \(24.3216\). Expanding the numerator only through degree two would have kept just the constant after division and lost both needed higher terms.

examples.title: A coefficient becomes a quadratic model on a restricted domain
examples.question: Let \(C(k)\) be the coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+kx)^3(1+(3-k)x)^2\), where \(0<k<3\). Find the range of \(C\), then solve \(C(k)=19\) in the allowed domain.
solution: Only \(k=1\) belongs to \((0,3)\). Neither range endpoint is attained because the parameter interval excludes both endpoints.

examples.title: Require two distinct positive parameter values
examples.question: The coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+kx)^2(1+(k-2)x)^2\) is \(m\). Find the values of \(m\) for which the coefficient equation has two distinct positive solutions for \(k\).
solution:
The larger root is then positive. The smaller root must also be positive:

\[1-\sqrt{\frac{m+2}{6}}>0\Longrightarrow\frac{m+2}{6}<1\Longrightarrow m<4.\]
At \(m=-2\), there is one repeated root \(k=1\). At \(m=4\), the roots are \(0\) and \(2\). These boundaries fail “two distinct positive”, so both inequalities are strict.

extraPractice.title: Match the small input to the base
extraPractice.prompt: Use the terms through \(x^2\) in \((1+x)^5\) to estimate \(1.02^5\). Give the substituted value of \(x\) and the value of the retained polynomial.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[x=0.02,\qquad Q_2(x)=1+5x+10x^2.\]
  2. \[Q_2(0.02)=1+0.1+0.004=1.104.\]

  3. Thus \(1.02^5\approx1.104\) with this specified truncation. The omitted positive terms mean this estimate is below the true value.

extraPractice.title: Keep the non-unit base in every coefficient
extraPractice.prompt: Use terms through \(x^2\) in \((3+x)^4\) to estimate \(3.01^4\). Enter the constant term of the expansion and the value of this retained polynomial.
extraPractice.hint: Use \(x=0.01\). The first three terms are \(3^4+4(3^3)x+6(3^2)x^2\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[(3+x)^4=81+108x+54x^2+12x^3+x^4.\]
  2. \[Q_2(0.01)=81+1.08+0.0054=82.0854.\]

  3. The constant is \(81\), and the requested estimate is \(82.0854\). This is the value of the truncation; a separate error check is needed for any claimed rounding accuracy.

extraPractice.title: A negative input can reverse the error sign
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(F(x)=(1+x)^4\), \(Q_2(x)=1+4x+6x^2\), and \(R(x)=F(x)-Q_2(x)\). Find \(R(-0.1)\) exactly. Does \(Q_2(-0.1)\) overestimate or underestimate \(F(-0.1)\)?
extraPractice.hint: Keep the sign when cubing the input. The remainder is \(4x^3+x^4\).

extraPractice.title: Bound every omitted term on an interval
extraPractice.prompt: For \(0\le x\le0.05\), approximate \((1+x)^5\) by \(Q_2(x)=1+5x+10x^2\). Find the maximum absolute error over this interval and the value of \(x\) where it occurs.
extraPractice.hint: The remainder is \(10x^3+5x^4+x^5\). Every term is nonnegative and increases as \(x\) increases on the stated interval.

extraPractice.title: Check the rounding interval
extraPractice.prompt: For \(F(x)=(1+x)^4\), use \(Q_2(x)=1+4x+6x^2\) and its exact remainder to determine \(1.01^4\) correct to four decimal places. Give the absolute error of \(Q_2(0.01)\) as well.

fields.label: Exact absolute error of the quadratic estimate

extraPractice.hint: Find \(Q_2(0.01)\) and \(4(0.01)^3+(0.01)^4\). Compare the corrected value with the rounding boundaries around the proposed answer.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[Q_2(0.01)=1.0406,\qquad R(0.01)=0.00000401.\]
  2. \[1.01^4=1.04060401.\]

  3. This value lies strictly between \(1.04055\) and \(1.04065\), so it rounds to \(1.0406\) to four decimal places. The error is \(0.00000401\).

  4. In other problems, inspect the interval around the actual estimate; a small error must not cross a rounding boundary.

extraPractice.title: Truncate after the negative-power shift
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x\ne0\), define \(F(x)=\frac{(1+x)^5-1-5x}{x^2}\). Retain the constant and linear terms of \(F\) to estimate \(F(0.02)\). Find that estimate and its exact absolute error.
extraPractice.hint: Division by \(x^2\) lowers every numerator exponent by two. The cubic term of the numerator becomes the linear term in \(F\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[(1+x)^5-1-5x=10x^2+10x^3+5x^4+x^5.\]
  2. \[F(x)=10+10x+5x^2+x^3\qquad(x\ne0).\]
  3. \[Q_1(0.02)=10.2,\qquad R(0.02)=5(0.02)^2+(0.02)^3=0.002008.\]

  4. The error is positive, so its absolute value is \(0.002008\). The original expression remains undefined at \(x=0\).

starters.title: Find the fewest terms that meet an error target
starters.question: Approximate \(1.04^5\) by retaining the first terms in ascending powers of \(x\) from \((1+x)^5\), with \(x=0.04\). Find the lowest retained degree giving an absolute error less than \(0.00001\). State the number of terms, the resulting approximation and its exact error.
starters.hint: Test the remainder after the cubic term and after the quartic term. At this positive input every omitted term is positive.
starters.solution:
1. \[(1+x)^5=1+5x+10x^2+10x^3+5x^4+x^5.\]

  2. After degree three the error is

    \[5(0.04)^4+(0.04)^5=0.0000129024>0.00001.\]

  3. After degree four the error is

    \[(0.04)^5=0.0000001024<0.00001.\]

  4. Earlier truncations omit these positive terms and additional positive terms, so they also fail. Degree four is therefore the lowest possible degree, giving five retained terms.

  5. \[Q_4(0.04)=1+0.2+0.016+0.00064+0.0000128=1.2166528.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain the needed finite expansion and omitted terms.
  • 1 mark: show that the cubic truncation fails the error target.
  • 1 mark: show that the quartic truncation meets the target.
  • 1 mark: justify minimality and identify five retained terms.
  • 1 mark: give the approximation and its exact error.

starters.title: Translate bracket restrictions into a coefficient range
starters.question:
Let \(C(k)\) be the coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+kx)^4(1+(2-k)x)^2\). Both linear coefficients inside the two brackets are strictly positive.

Show on paper that \(C(k)=4+12k-k^2\). Find the exact range of \(C\), state whether either endpoint is attained, and find every allowed \(k\) for which \(C(k)=13\).
starters.hint: The bracket conditions give \(0<k<2\). Extract all three quadratic contributions and complete the square in \(k\).
starters.solution:
1. \[C(k)=6k^2+8k(2-k)+(2-k)^2=4+12k-k^2.\]
  2. \[C(k)=40-(k-6)^2.\]

  3. For \(0<k<2\), we have \(-6<k-6<-4\), so \(16<(k-6)^2<36\). Thus the exact range is

    \[4<C(k)<24.\]

    Every intermediate value is attained because this quadratic is continuous and strictly increasing on the interval. Neither endpoint is included.

  4. \[C(k)=13\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(k-6)^2=27\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=6\pm3\sqrt{3}.\]

  5. Only \(6-3\sqrt{3}\) lies between \(0\) and \(2\). The positive-sign candidate violates the bracket conditions.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain all three contributions to the quadratic coefficient.
  • 1 mark: simplify and complete the square.
  • 1 mark: translate the positive bracket coefficients into \(0<k<2\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the open coefficient range \((4,24)\).
  • 1 mark: obtain both algebraic candidates from \(C(k)=13\).
  • 1 mark: retain only \(6-3\sqrt{3}\) after checking the original restrictions.

starters.title: A minimum can be attained while the required interval is open
starters.question:
The coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+kx)^3(1+(k-1)x)^3\) is \(m\), where \(k\) and \(m\) are real.

Find the range of \(m\) for which the coefficient equation has two distinct positive values of \(k\). Explain both excluded endpoints. Then find those two values when \(m=0\).
starters.hint: Extract the coefficient as \(15k^2-15k+3\). Its minimum controls distinct real roots. Use the smaller root from the completed-square form to check that both are positive.
starters.solution:
1. \[m=3k^2+9k(k-1)+3(k-1)^2=15k^2-15k+3.\]
  2. \[m=15\left(k-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2-\frac{3}{4}.\]

  3. Two distinct real solutions require \(m>-\frac{3}{4}\). Write \(d=\sqrt{\frac{m+\frac{3}{4}}{15}}>0\). The roots are \(k=\frac{1}{2}\pm d\). Both are positive exactly when the smaller one is positive:

    \[\frac{1}{2}-d>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{m+\frac{3}{4}}{15}<\frac{1}{4}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m<3.\]
  4. \[-\frac{3}{4}<m<3.\]

  5. At \(m=-\frac{3}{4}\), the minimum is attained, but there is only the repeated solution \(k=\frac{1}{2}\). At \(m=3\), the roots are \(0\) and \(1\), so one is not strictly positive. Both endpoints are excluded for the stated question.

  6. For \(m=0\),

    \[5k^2-5k+1=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{5}}{10}.\]

    Both values are positive and distinct.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain \(15k^2-15k+3\) from the product.
  • 1 mark: find the minimum \(-\frac{3}{4}\) by completing the square.
  • 1 mark: require a strict lower bound for two distinct roots.
  • 1 mark: use positivity of both roots to obtain \(m<3\).
  • 1 mark: explain why the zero root excludes the upper endpoint.
  • 1 mark: state the complete open interval and explain the repeated-root endpoint.
  • 1 mark: obtain both exact positive roots when \(m=0\).

revision.body:
A full finite expansion is exact; a short estimate needs a remainder check.

Match the input and measure the error

Solve for the input from the target base. If factoring out \(a\), retain the multiplier \(a^n\).

\[P=Q+R,\qquad\text{absolute error}=|R|.\]

\(R>0\): underestimate; \(R<0\): overestimate. Percentage error is \(100\frac{|R|}{|P|}\%\) for \(P\ne0\). Finite identities have no infinite-series convergence restriction.

Bound, count and round

\[R(x)=\sum c_rx^r,\ |x|\le h\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |R(x)|\le\sum|c_r|h^r.\]

For positive powers, bound every omitted term. To prove the least degree, show it passes and shorter choices fail. Count the constant as a term. To guarantee rounding, the whole true-value interval must stay within one pair of rounding boundaries.

Expand far enough before simplifying

An outside \(x^{-s}\) lowers degrees by \(s\): a final degree \(j\) may need inner degree \(j+s\). Subtract cancellations before identifying the final remainder. Preserve original denominator restrictions.

Coupled coefficient models

Collect every product contribution, complete the square, and apply the original parameter interval. Check both solution branches and whether range endpoints are attained.

\[6(k-1)^2-2=m\Longrightarrow k=1\pm\sqrt{\frac{m+2}{6}}.\]

Two distinct positive roots require \(m>-2\) and the smaller root positive, giving \(m<4\). Thus \(-2<m<4\); verify each excluded boundary.
revision.checks:
• Correct substituted input and outside factor?
  • Every omitted term included in the error?
  • Strict accuracy and rounding boundaries checked?
  • All parameter branches and endpoint conditions checked?
